datasets.title: Google search-ad costs for lawyer searches by practice area and state: top-of-page bid bands and competition (Google Ads Keyword Planner)
datasets.summary: What advertisers bid to show at the top of Google for lawyer searches, practice by practice. For 86 query families (English and Spanish) in the whole US, all 50 states and DC, the file gives the top-of-page bid band of each family's English and Spanish head query (Google Keyword Planner's low and high top-of-page bid estimates: the range advertisers have historically bid to show above the results), the competition level and index, plus the family's median low and high bids across its queries. Figures come from Google Ads Keyword Planner (October 2025 to September 2026) and are shown as bands with that period; for the US and 27 states, a DataForSEO pull of the same Google Ads data agrees on every bid band it shares. For the US, families are grouped into demand tiers by searches a month with the median high bid of each tier. Our own anonymized benchmark of what law-firm clicks actually cost is linked as a separate measure and never mixed into these figures.
datasets.uses: Use it to budget search ads before launch: the band says what a click at the top of the page has cost in a state, the Spanish head shows whether Spanish searches are cheaper, and competition says how many advertisers bid. A bid band is the auction's history for the 12 months before the as-of date, not a quote: your own cost depends on quality, match type, hours and place. For what law firms really paid per click on live campaigns, see Probative benchmarks, 2025–2026 (figures are approximate and shown as ranges).

datasets.title: Attorneys by county in Ohio, California, Michigan, Idaho, Arizona, Washington and Pennsylvania, from each bar's public counts
datasets.summary: How many lawyers each bar counts in each county, for seven states. Ohio: attorneys by county of address and status, from the Supreme Court of Ohio's attorney directory list (88 counties, with admission decade, private practice and Spanish speakers). California: active, inactive, judge and not-eligible licensees in each of the 58 counties, from the State Bar's county table. Michigan: active State Bar members living in each of the 83 counties, with private practice and the change from 2024. Idaho: members by status in each of the seven judicial districts. Arizona: active State Bar members in each of the 15 counties (the Bar's 2022 report). Washington: WSBA licensees of every type (lawyers plus limited licensees) in each of the 39 counties, with the attorney counts by member type. Pennsylvania: active attorneys in the seven counties the Disciplinary Board's annual report lists, and the Board's statewide status counts. Each record carries the source's own as-of date and a rate per 10,000 residents from the Census Bureau's county estimate. Only counts are published, and where a count is built from a directory file no name, birthdate, address or registration number is kept or written. In Ohio, counts in a disciplinary, deceased or other status, an admission decade, private practice or Spanish are published from five lawyers up, and only where no smaller count in the same group can be worked out from a county's total or the statewide figures. Every state record ties to its source's own total, and every published number is read a second time from the source file before release.
datasets.uses: Use it to see how many lawyers already serve a county before choosing where to advertise: active attorneys per 10,000 residents, how many are inactive or retired, and for some states how many are in private practice or admitted recently. The seven bars count differently: the unit of each record is printed with it (active attorneys with an address in the county, active members living in the county, or all members of every license type), the as-of date differs by state and a county is where the lawyer's address is, not where clients live. Compare counties within a state, not one state's count with another's.
datasets.attribution: Source: Probative, Attorneys by county in Ohio, California, Michigan, Idaho, Arizona, Washington and Pennsylvania, from each bar's public counts, version 2.0.0, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23962861, licensed CC BY 4.0.

datasets.citeAs: Probative Growth, Attorneys by county in Ohio, California, Michigan, Idaho, Arizona, Washington and Pennsylvania, from each bar's public counts, 2026, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23962861
datasets.disclaimer: Not legal advice. These are counts of lawyers from state bars' and courts' public count pages, reports and directory, kept for research and marketing planning. A status is the bar's record, not a judgment of any lawyer's skill or standing, and a county is the county of the address the lawyer gave, not where the lawyer practices or where clients live. Rights and deadlines in a matter are for your own counsel.

datasets.title: Civil aviation accidents by state, year and type of operation (NTSB), 2008 to 2026
datasets.summary: Civil aviation accidents in the United States investigated by the National Transportation Safety Board, for the nation and for each state, DC, Puerto Rico and Guam in each year from 2008 to September 2026: accidents, fatal accidents, deaths, serious and minor injuries, and the accidents and deaths by type of operation of the first aircraft (general aviation, airlines, commuter and on-demand, agricultural, other). NTSB incidents, accidents abroad, narratives and probable causes are not included. Accidents offshore or with no state are counted in the national record only.
datasets.uses: Use it to size aviation-injury demand by state: where accidents and deaths concentrate, how general aviation compares with commercial flying, and how counts moved from year to year, as context for aviation-accident and wrongful-death work. Agents can look up a state, compare several, or search by year or place.
datasets.attribution: Source: Probative, Civil aviation accidents by state, year and type of operation (NTSB), 2008 to 2026, version 2.0.0, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23962878, licensed CC BY 4.0.

datasets.citeAs: Probative Growth, Civil aviation accidents by state, year and type of operation (NTSB), 2008 to 2026, 2026, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23962878
datasets.disclaimer: Not legal advice. These are counts of accidents recorded by the NTSB, not findings of fault: a probable cause, if any, is in the NTSB's own report. An accident is an event meeting the NTSB's definition, which includes events with no injury. Counts for the latest year are preliminary and are revised as the NTSB closes cases. Claims and deadlines are for your own counsel.

datasets.mcpLine: NTSB civil aviation accidents by state and year, 2008 to 2026: accidents, deaths, injuries and type of operation.
datasets.measurementTechnique: The NTSB publishes its aviation accident database as a downloadable Access file rebuilt monthly. Each U.S. accident (not incident) is counted once in its state and year, by the type of operation (FAR part) of its first aircraft; deaths, serious and minor injuries are the event totals. Only counts are kept: narratives, names, registrations, places and times are dropped. A gate re-derives the totals from the person-level injury table of the same file, re-downloads the file and re-derives 50 random state-year cells.

datasets.title: Bankruptcy filings by chapter, court district, state and county, quarterly (U.S. Courts)
datasets.summary: Bankruptcy cases commenced in the 12 months ending on each quarter-end, from the U.S. Courts' Tables F-5A (by county and chapter), F-2 (by court district, chapter and business or nonbusiness debt) and F (cases filed, terminated and pending). One record per area: the United States, every state, DC and territory, 93 court districts and about 3,100 counties. Each gives the latest period's cases by Chapter 7, 11, 13 and other chapters, the business and nonbusiness split, the change on the year before, filings per 1,000 residents (Census 2025 population estimates) and the court's figures for the six earlier periods. Every table is checked against the court's own totals row. Counts of cases, not outcomes: a filing is not a discharge.
datasets.uses: Use it to see where debt trouble reaches the federal bankruptcy courts, how Chapter 7 and Chapter 13 mix in a state or county, and which districts are growing, before you size a bankruptcy practice's market. It counts cases commenced, not people helped or fees earned.
datasets.attribution: Source: Probative, Bankruptcy filings by chapter, court district, state and county, quarterly (U.S. Courts), version 2.0.0, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23962892, licensed CC BY 4.0.

datasets.citeAs: Probative Growth, Bankruptcy filings by chapter, court district, state and county, quarterly (U.S. Courts), 2026, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23962892
datasets.disclaimer: Not legal advice. These are counts from the courts' published statistics, kept for marketing planning. A filing is not a discharge or an outcome, and the courts revise the tables as their database updates; check the current table at uscourts.gov.

datasets.mcpLine: Bankruptcy filings by chapter, court district, state and county, quarterly from U.S. Courts tables F-5A, F-2 and F.
datasets.measurementTechnique: Each 12-month table is downloaded from uscourts.gov and read by a script. A table counts only if its county rows add up to the court's own Total row and to each district's row, and the district rows add up to the Total row; a period that fails is kept at district level only. State rows sum the counties by the debtor's state. Rates divide cases by the Census July 1, 2025 population estimate.

datasets.title: The new-lawyer pipeline by jurisdiction: bar exam pass rates and new admissions, 2025
datasets.summary: For every US jurisdiction that reports to the National Conference of Bar Examiners (the 50 states, DC, Guam, the Northern Mariana Islands, Palau, Puerto Rico and the Virgin Islands): the overall 2025 bar exam pass rate, how many new lawyers were admitted in 2025 (by examination, by transferred UBE score and on motion), how admissions by exam or transferred score changed since 2021, and how much of the total came from transferred scores and from motion. NCBE reserves its published tables, so this dataset republishes none of them: every figure is one we derive from them (a rate, a sum, a change, a share), credited to NCBE with a link to the table it comes from. Each jurisdiction's rows add up to NCBE's own totals row before anything is published.
datasets.uses: Use it to size the new-lawyer market in a state: how many people are licensed each year, how many arrive by passing the exam, by moving a score or by moving their license, and whether that supply is growing. A state with a falling count and a low pass rate is losing new lawyers to its neighbours. Read it beside the lawyer wages and law-offices datasets before you decide where to recruit or advertise to new lawyers.

datasets.title: Probative benchmarks, 2025–2026
datasets.summary: Probative benchmarks, 2025–2026: our data on law-firm marketing. Figures are approximate and shown as ranges: bands, named tiers and rounded values, one table per file. The public tables cover how quickly inquiries become signed clients, phone calls and signed clients, AI answers and organic search clicks, search-ad click costs, what people type, calls from ads, Local Services Ads leads, inquiries by quarter and ad cost per signed client. Each row gives the measure, the band or tier, its unit and a rough size band. Read the band, not a point. The methods page defines every measure. Five injury-case tables were added in version 5.0.0 (each row states its version): Google Ads cost per click-traced lead and signed client, the non-brand click cost and the fourth-quarter dip, the Google Ads budget split, and Local Services Ads lead timing, charges and call lengths.
datasets.uses: Use it to compare your own firm's figure with a band, not to predict a result: a band is a range and a tier is a named range, so a firm above or below it is a prompt to look closer, not proof of a problem.

datasets.title: Recreational boating accidents by state and year: incidents, deaths, injuries and damage (U.S. Coast Guard), 2019 to 2024
datasets.summary: Recreational boating incidents reported to the U.S. Coast Guard, for the nation and for each state, DC and territory in each year from 2019 to 2024: incidents, fatal incidents, incidents with a non-fatal injury, property-damage-only incidents, deaths, people injured and property damage in dollars. The Coast Guard called these accidents until its 2024 report and now calls them incidents. Incidents offshore (Atlantic, Pacific, Gulf) are in the national record only. Each year comes from that year's Coast Guard report.
datasets.uses: Use it to size boating-injury demand by state: where incidents, deaths and injuries concentrate, how the count changed since 2019 and how much damage follows, as context for boating, maritime-injury and wrongful-death work. Agents can look up a state, compare several, or search by year or place.

datasets.title: New business applications by county (Census Business Formation Statistics)
datasets.summary: Business applications (requests for a new Employer Identification Number) in every U.S. county from 2005 to 2025, with each county's latest count, the change over a year and since 2019, and the sums for each state and the nation, from the Census Bureau's Business Formation Statistics annual county file. The Census Bureau applied differentially private noise to the June 2026 release, so every record is flagged noise; county sums are checked against the Bureau's own monthly state series.
datasets.uses: Use it to see where new businesses are being started: which counties take in the most new-business applications, how fast that is growing, and how a county compares with its state. Each application is a likely client for business formation, contracts and employment advice. Pair it with the law-offices and legal-need datasets by county FIPS code. Agents can look up a state and its counties, compare up to ten states, or search a county by name.

datasets.title: California court filings by county: civil, criminal, family, juvenile, probate and appeals, fiscal years 2023–24 and 2024–25
datasets.summary: How many cases were filed in each of California's 58 superior courts (one per county) and statewide, by case type, from the Judicial Council of California's Court Statistics Reports: unlimited civil (motor-vehicle injury, other injury and wrongful death, other civil), limited civil, unlawful detainer, small claims, felonies and misdemeanors, family law, juvenile, probate, mental health and appeals. One record per county and case type, with the prior year beside it. In every table the 58 counties add up exactly to the report's own statewide row, and the totals inside each row add up too. Counts only: no lawyer or firm is listed or ranked.
datasets.uses: Use it to see where the legal work is. A filing is a new case opened in the county's superior court, so the counts show how much demand each practice area has in each county; they do not show how many of those people hired a lawyer. Filings are for a state fiscal year (July 1 to June 30). Compare a county's count with the statewide row and with the year before, and read the report's own limits before you rely on a small county's figure. To size a California market before you spend, compare one county's civil unlimited and limited filings with its neighbors': where filings run high for the population, there are more disputes looking for a lawyer, and where they fall from one fiscal year to the next, demand may be moving elsewhere.
datasets.attribution: Source: Probative, California court filings by county: civil, criminal, family, juvenile, probate and appeals, fiscal years 2023–24 and 2024–25, version 2.0.0, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23963026, licensed CC BY 4.0.

datasets.title: Deadlines to file an employment-discrimination charge: the federal EEOC limit and each state agency's own limit
datasets.summary: How long a worker has to file a charge of employment discrimination: the EEOC's 180-day limit and its 300-day extension, and the limit each covered state's own statute sets for its civil-rights agency. The federal limit is the EEOC's own page; a state row is the statute's words or the state agency's own statement of its limit. datasets.title: Federal civil filings by nature of suit and district, 12-month periods since 2018
datasets.summary: How many civil cases were filed in each of the 94 U.S. district courts and nationwide, by nature of suit, from the Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts' Statistical Tables for the Federal Judiciary: Table C-3 (the 94 districts by case type: contract, real property, torts, civil rights, prisoner petitions, labor, Social Security, intellectual property and more, U.S. cases and private cases) and Table C-2 (the nation by about 100 natures of suit, such as product liability, medical malpractice, employment, the Fair Labor Standards Act, ERISA and consumer credit, with the basis of jurisdiction). One record per district and case type for the latest 12 months, with the year before and the history of every earlier table, and one record per nature of suit nationwide. In every table the 94 districts add up exactly to the national Total row, every circuit adds up to its districts and every nature-of-suit group adds up to the rows under it. Counts only: no lawyer or firm is listed or ranked.
datasets.uses: Use it to see where federal civil cases are filed and which kinds are growing. A filing is a civil case commenced in a district court in the 12-month period, so the counts show how much federal demand each case type has in each district; they do not show how many of those people hired a lawyer, and they leave out state courts. Prisoner petitions are kept apart from the injury, employment and consumer groups. Compare a district's count with the nation and with the year before, and read the flag on small counts before you rely on a percent change.

datasets.title: CFPB complaints about debt collection, credit reporting and debt management, by state and month
datasets.summary: Complaints that consumers filed with the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) about debt collection, credit reporting and credit repair, and debt or credit management, counted by state, month, product and issue from January 2018, with the last 12 months set against the 12 before and per 100,000 residents. One record per state, DC, Puerto Rico and territory for each of the three product groups, with the share of complaints the company answered on time and the issue people raised most. The counts come from the CFPB's own Consumer Complaint Database search API, as aggregates, so no complaint, narrative, company name or ZIP code is ever copied; for every month the issue counts add up to the bureau's own count for each product group. The bureau changed its credit-reporting product name twice; every name is combined into one group. Complaints are consumers' own reports, not findings of any violation.
datasets.uses: Use it to see where consumers report the most trouble with debt collectors, credit bureaus and debt-management firms, and how that has moved, before you plan marketing for a consumer-law practice. Look up your state: the record gives the last 12 months of complaints for one product group, the rate per 100,000 residents, the change from the 12 months before, the on-time response share, the most common issue and 36 monthly counts. Read the rate as how often people in a state file complaints, not how often a law is broken.

datasets.title: FTC Consumer Sentinel reports by state: fraud, identity theft and imposter scams, 2024 Data Book
datasets.summary: Reports that consumers made to the U.S. Federal Trade Commission's Consumer Sentinel Network in 2024, by state, DC and Puerto Rico, from the FTC's Consumer Sentinel Network Data Book 2024. Four records per jurisdiction: fraud and other reports and identity theft reports (each with the count, the rate per 100,000 people and the FTC's rank among the 50 states), imposter-scam reports (the share of the state's reports that the FTC prints, with a count and a rate derived from it, flagged as rounded) and fraud reports with the share reporting a loss, the total dollars reported lost and the median loss. Four national records give the whole country. A report is what a consumer or partner told the FTC, not a finding; the state tables leave out reports from state-specific data contributors and reports with no state.
datasets.uses: Use it to see how many fraud, identity-theft and imposter-scam reports each state's consumers send the FTC, and how a state compares per 100,000 people, before you plan consumer-protection or fraud-recovery marketing. Look up your state: the records give each count, rate and rank as the FTC prints them. The imposter-scam count is derived from a whole percent, so it is a rounded estimate and is flagged. A firm weighing a new fraud-recovery or identity-theft page can rank the states it is licensed in by reports per resident: a high rate with a small population can mean a crowded field of victims and few firms speaking to them, while the imposter-scam share hints at which story to lead the page with.

datasets.mcpLine: FTC Consumer Sentinel reports by state: fraud, identity theft and imposter scams per 100,000 people (2024 Data Book).
datasets.measurementTechnique: The FTC's Consumer Sentinel Network Data Book is read from the FTC's PDF by machine in layout mode: the two State Rankings tables, one page per state, Appendix C and the national tables. Counts stay exactly as the FTC prints them. The imposter-scam count is the printed whole-percent share times the state's reports (fraud and other plus identity theft, a base checked against the identity-theft share on every page), flagged noise with its margin. A release gate checks that the ranks reproduce from the rates, that each state page prints the table's counts and ranks, that the two tables imply one population, that Appendix C losses match each page, and that the states add up to no more than the country.

datasets.title: County income and migration from IRS tax returns
datasets.summary: Individual income tax returns, individuals, adjusted gross income, salaries and wages in every U.S. county for the latest tax year, with the change in income per return from the year before, and the returns and income that moved into and out of each county and state between two filing years, from the IRS Statistics of Income county and migration files. County returns are rounded to the nearest 10 and migration flows are published from 20 returns up; every figure is kept as published, never estimated.
datasets.uses: Use it to see how much income a county has and how fast it is moving, and where income is arriving from or leaving to: returns and adjusted gross income per county, the change over a year, and net migration from other states. These are the denominators for estate planning, tax, real estate and business law practices. Pair it with the legal-need and law-offices datasets by county FIPS code. Agents can look up a state and its counties, compare up to ten states, or search a county by name.

datasets.citeAs: Probative Growth, County income and migration from IRS tax returns, 2026, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23963195
datasets.disclaimer: Not legal advice. These are totals from filed individual tax returns, not a county's wealth, a person's income or a prediction of who needs a lawyer, and migration shows where filers' addresses changed, not why. Questions about taxes, estates or property are for a licensed attorney or tax professional.

datasets.measurementTechnique: Read from the IRS Statistics of Income all-returns county file and the county and state migration files, kept row for row; the IRS state rows are used as published and the US row is the sum of the states. datasets.title: Crime and arrests by county and state: violent and property crime, DUI and drug arrests (FBI)
datasets.summary: What police agencies reported to the FBI over the last five complete calendar years, for every state and for 2,981 counties, home to 96.5% of U.S. residents: violent crimes, property crimes, arrests for driving under the influence, all arrests, and, for states, arrests for drug abuse violations. County rows add up the agencies the FBI places in each county (a city police department, a sheriff's office, a campus force; an agency that serves several counties counts in the county of its headquarters); a row says how many agencies there are and what share of the county's residents they cover, because each county counts only the months its agencies reported (never a zero in their place), and a county-year appears when at least one of its agencies reported. Rates are per 100,000 residents of the agencies that did report. State rows are the FBI's own state series; the county rows add up the agency-level answers, which can come to less than the state series where the FBI's state count includes reports its agency-level answers do not return. The United States row is the sum of the states. Only counts are published: no officer, victim, suspect or agency name.
datasets.uses: Use it to size criminal-defense and DUI work in the counties a firm serves: how many DUI and drug arrests agencies report there each year, how that compares with violent and property crime, how the rate per 100,000 residents compares with the state and the country, and how complete the reporting is. Look up a state to get every county in it, compare up to ten states, or search for a county by name. These are what agencies reported to the FBI, not all crime: an arrest is not a conviction, and a county with low coverage is understated.
datasets.attribution: Source: Probative, Crime and arrests by county and state: violent and property crime, DUI and drug arrests (FBI), version 2.0.0, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23963245, licensed CC BY 4.0.
datasets.citation: Probative. (2026). Crime and arrests by county and state: violent and property crime, DUI and drug arrests (FBI) (Version 2.0.0) [Data set]. Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23963245
datasets.citeAs: Probative Growth, Crime and arrests by county and state: violent and property crime, DUI and drug arrests (FBI), 2026, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23963245
datasets.disclaimer: Not legal advice. These are counts of crimes and arrests that police agencies reported to the FBI, kept for research and marketing planning. An arrest says an officer took someone into custody, not that a charge was filed or proved. Whether and how to defend a charge, and every deadline, are for the person's own counsel.

datasets.mcpLine: FBI violent and property crime, DUI and drug arrests by county and state, five years, with how many agencies reported.
datasets.measurementTechnique: FBI Crime Data Explorer monthly counts for every agency the FBI lists in the 50 states and DC (violent-crime and property-crime offenses, DUI and all arrests) are summed by calendar year and placed in the county the agency lists, or, for an agency that lists several counties, the listed county that holds its headquarters (Census Bureau geocoder); only the months an agency reported are counted, and rates use the residents of the agencies that reported. State rows are the FBI's own state series: the county rows never exceed them, and the gap is printed by the release check; the FBI's national rate, scaled to the share of residents covered, is the second check on the total.

datasets.title: Federal criminal cases by offense and district (U.S. Courts Tables D-1, D-2 and D-3)
datasets.summary: Criminal defendants whose cases were opened in the 94 federal district courts, counted from the Statistical Tables for the Federal Judiciary that the Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts publishes for each 12-month period ending June 30 and December 31. Each record gives one district, one state with more than one district, or the whole country, for one period: the defendants commenced (transfers between districts left out), split by offense into nineteen columns and ten offense groups, with drug, immigration (illegal reentry shown on its own), firearms, fraud, sex offenses and traffic picked out, the felony, Class A misdemeanor and petty-offense split from Table D-1, and the same period a year earlier. National records add Table D-2's detail of about a hundred offenses, from bank robbery and health-care fraud to drunk driving on federal land. Every period's districts add up to the national total printed by the Courts, and every district ties to Table D-1.
datasets.uses: Use it to size the federal criminal-defense market where a firm practises: how many people are charged in each federal district each year, with what (drug trafficking, illegal reentry, gun possession, fraud, child exploitation, traffic on federal land), how many face a felony, and whether the count is rising. Look up a state to get every district in it, compare up to ten states, or search for a district by name. Federal cases are a small share of all criminal cases, so read it alongside state court filings.

datasets.title: Legal market crosswalks: practice areas, federal case codes, states, federal districts and counties
datasets.summary: The shared keys that join every Probative dataset. One record per practice area (our taxonomy of consumer and business practice areas, each linked to the FOLIO Area of Law class it matches, the federal nature-of-suit codes of its cases, the site's practice pages and the datasets that measure its demand, supply, rules and money), per federal nature-of-suit code, per state and territory (FIPS and postal codes, Census region and division, federal circuit and districts), per federal judicial district (our district key, the Federal Judicial Center code and the court's CM/ECF id), per county and county equivalent in the 50 states, DC and the territories (Puerto Rico's municipios and the county equivalents of Guam, the U.S. Virgin Islands, the Northern Mariana Islands, American Samoa and Midway: FIPS code, the federal district and statutory division it belongs to, its metro or micro area and its Census population), per former county code older sources still use (with the current counties that took its area), and per documented source code that names a place under another key (EEOC's WQ for Wake Island) or is not a place at all (military mail, the freely associated states, the VA's unplaced addresses, U.S. Courts' outside-the-U.S. code). Every county's district is read from the statute and checked against the counties U.S. Courts lists under each district in its bankruptcy Table F-5A.
datasets.uses: Use it to join any two Probative datasets, or our data with your own: a county FIPS code gives the federal district whose filings and bankruptcy figures apply to it, a practice area gives the federal case codes and the datasets that measure it, and a district key gives the counties and population it covers. Agents can resolve a place or a practice to the right keys before calling any other Probative dataset.

datasets.measurementTechnique: Counties and populations come from the Census Bureau's vintage 2025 estimates (Puerto Rico's municipios from its vintage 2025 municipio estimates, the other territories' county equivalents from the Census 2020 county code list with their 2020 Census counts); each county's federal district and division is read from 28 U.S.C. chapter 5 (Virginia's independent cities by section 127(c)) and checked against the counties U.S. Courts lists under each district in Table F-5A; circuits from 28 U.S.C. section 41; the territories' districts from 28 U.S.C. section 119 and 48 U.S.C. sections 644a, 1424, 1611 and 1821; former county codes and their successors from the Census county code lists, its Substantial Changes to Counties pages and its Connecticut crosswalk; metro areas from the July 2023 OMB delineation; nature-of-suit codes from the U.S. Courts code descriptions (Rev. 06/26); practice areas and their links are Probative's own classification, mapped to FOLIO class ids.

datasets.title: Demand per law office, by state: residents, bankruptcy cases, fatal crashes, divorces, Spanish speakers and evictions for each law office
datasets.summary: Where there is the most legal demand for each law office. Five public datasets joined by state: private law-office establishments (2026 Q1, 177,138 in the 51 states) against residents, bankruptcy cases commenced (12 months ending 2026-09-30), fatal crashes (2024), divorces in the last 12 months and Spanish speakers with limited English (ACS 2020-2024), and eviction filings for the 23 states with recent eviction data. Each state is placed in the highest, middle or lowest third on every ratio and overall.
datasets.uses: Use it to see where demand is high for each existing law office, so you know where a new market, a new practice area or more ad spend has the most demand behind it. A ratio is demand events divided by the state's law offices; the row says how many law offices it rests on.

datasets.title: Legal deserts: law offices and lawyers per resident in every U.S. county
datasets.summary: Which counties have few or no law offices for their residents, under two definitions shown side by side. Offices: private law-office establishments per 10,000 residents (BLS QCEW, latest quarter, 2025 population), flagged when under 1 or when there is none. Lawyers: where a state's own bar or court publishes a county count (California, New York, Mississippi, Illinois), lawyers per 1,000 residents, flagged when under 1, the threshold the American Bar Association used in 2020. Each county also shows the Census count of solo legal-services firms with no employees, and whether it is in a metropolitan area, a smaller city area or neither. State and national rows count the counties. Bar figures are county-by-status totals only; no lawyer is named.
datasets.uses: Find counties with no office, compare a county with its state, or count residents living in thin-coverage counties. Both definitions are counts and rates, not findings about access to justice: bar addresses of record are not where a lawyer practises, and a nearby county's offices may serve the county.

datasets.title: Medical device adverse event reports by product code and quarter (FDA MAUDE via openFDA)
datasets.summary: Adverse event reports the FDA received about medical devices, counted by device product code and calendar quarter from 2025 Q1: reports, deaths, injuries, malfunctions and other, for the 300 product codes with the most reports and for all devices together. Counted with the openFDA device event API (licence CC0); no report row, narrative, patient or manufacturer is ever read, only counts. Reports are filed up to weeks after an event and are driven by litigation and recalls as well as by harm, so a count is not an incidence rate.
datasets.uses: Use it to see which device types draw the most adverse event reports and how that moves quarter to quarter: a sudden jump in injury reports for one product code is often the first public sign of a recall or a mass tort. Product-liability and mass-tort practices can watch the codes behind the devices they litigate. Pair it with the mdl dataset. Agents can look up the national total or a product code, compare quarters, or search a device by name.
datasets.attribution: Source: Probative, Medical device adverse event reports by product code and quarter (FDA MAUDE via openFDA), version 2.0.0, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23963431, licensed CC BY 4.0.

datasets.citeAs: Probative Growth, Medical device adverse event reports by product code and quarter (FDA MAUDE via openFDA), 2026, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23963431
datasets.disclaimer: Not legal advice. A report to the FDA is an allegation that a device may have caused or contributed to an event, not a finding that it did, and a count of reports is not an incidence rate or proof of a defect. Questions about an injury from a medical device are for a licensed product-liability attorney and the person's doctor.

datasets.title: Social Security disability hearing waits and workloads by hearing office
datasets.summary: How long Social Security disability claimants wait for a hearing before an administrative law judge, office by office, from the Social Security Administration's own public data files: the average months from the hearing request to the hearing for cases closed in the month, and each hearing office's fiscal-year-to-date receipts, dispositions, cases pending and average days from request to decision, with SSA's rank among 159 offices. Each record is one hearing office, with the state it sits in. Counts and averages only: no judge, claimant, lawyer or firm is named.
datasets.uses: Use it to see how long SSDI and SSI claimants in a market wait for a hearing, and how loaded the local hearing office is, before you plan disability intake and advertising there. A long wait means more claimants still looking for representation and a longer time before a fee is paid. Compare an office with the national median and with its neighbors. The averages are SSA's own; they describe cases already closed, not how long a new claimant will wait.

datasets.title: Serious drug adverse event reports by active ingredient (openFDA FAERS)
datasets.summary: Adverse event reports about drugs that reached the FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) and are served by openFDA, received 2024Q3 to 2026Q2: 2,649,395 reports in all, 1,430,033 serious and 197,378 with a death outcome. One record per active ingredient for the 312 ingredients with the most reports plus every ingredient named in an open multidistrict litigation (31 of them tagged with their MDL numbers): reports that list the ingredient, how many were serious, how many reported a death outcome, the same counts for each of the last eight quarters, and the five most reported reactions. National, one shard. A report names a drug and an event; it does not show that the drug caused the event, and FAERS holds duplicates, follow-ups and reports from outside the United States.
datasets.uses: Use it to see which drugs generate the most serious adverse event reports, how fast reports about an ingredient are rising or falling by quarter, and which reactions are reported most often, next to the open product-liability dockets that name the ingredient. Agents can look up the national record, compare ingredients and search by name.
datasets.attribution: Source: Probative, Serious drug adverse event reports by active ingredient (openFDA FAERS), version 2.0.0, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23963449, licensed CC BY 4.0.

datasets.citeAs: Probative Growth, Serious drug adverse event reports by active ingredient (openFDA FAERS), 2026, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23963449
datasets.disclaimer: Not legal advice. This is not medical advice either. A report in the FDA Adverse Event Reporting System is not proof that a drug caused an event; reports come from patients, clinicians and manufacturers, can be duplicated and are not verified. Questions about a medicine are for a health professional, and questions about an injury are for a licensed attorney.

datasets.measurementTechnique: Counted server-side on the openFDA drug adverse event API (api.fda.gov/drug/event.json): `count` on patient.drug.openfda.substance_name.exact by quarter of `receivedate` for all reports, serious reports (serious:1) and reports with a death outcome (seriousnessdeath:1), plus one count over the whole window and one per ingredient for its five most reported reactions. No report text or patient field is read. The window is the last eight complete quarters. An ingredient is counted once per report that lists it, whether as suspect, concomitant or interacting drug, in the name openFDA harmonizes it to (a salt form such as 'losartan potassium' is its own name; every name that is the ingredient plus only a salt word is kept). A gate asks openFDA for the all-drug totals again, checks that each ingredient's quarters add up to its window, and re-counts fifty random ingredient-period cells with a different query.

datasets.title: Employment discrimination charges to the EEOC, by state and basis, FY 2009 to FY 2025
datasets.summary: Charges of workplace discrimination received by the U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC), by state, DC, Puerto Rico and territory, fiscal year and basis (race, sex, national origin, religion, color, retaliation, age, disability, equal pay, genetic information and pregnancy under the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act), from the EEOC's Tables E1b and E1a. One record per jurisdiction and basis for the latest fiscal year, each with its count, its share of the state's charges, the rate per 100,000 private-sector workers (BLS Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages, from fiscal year 2014) and the whole FY 2009 to FY 2025 history. A charge can name more than one basis, so bases add up to more than the total, and charges filed only with a state or local fair-employment agency are not counted.
datasets.uses: Use it to see how many discrimination charges reach the EEOC from a state, which bases are cited most, and how that has moved over the years, before you plan employment-law marketing. Look up your state: the records give each basis for the latest fiscal year, its share of the state's charges and the rate per 100,000 private-sector workers, with the history. A state with its own fair-employment agency sends part of its charges there.
datasets.attribution: Source: Probative, Employment discrimination charges to the EEOC, by state and basis, FY 2009 to FY 2025, version 2.0.0, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23898101, licensed CC BY 4.0.

datasets.title: Eviction laws by state and territory: notice, cure, just cause, fees and timing (LSC)
datasets.summary: How the law of each U.S. state, the District of Columbia and five territories regulates residential evictions as of January 1, 2021, coded from the statutes by the Legal Services Corporation and Temple University's Center for Public Health Law Research: the notice a landlord must give before filing for nonpayment, whether a tenant may cure, whether a landlord needs a stated cause, caps on late fees, the filing fee the law sets, the days to answer, to appeal and between writ and removal, mediation, and the statute cited for the notice rule. One record per jurisdiction plus a national summary.
datasets.uses: Use it to compare how fast and how strictly each state lets a landlord move to evict, as context for landlord-tenant work and tenant-side or landlord-side marketing in a state. Agents can look up one state, compare several, or search by a rule ("just cause", "late fee"). The laws are those in effect on January 1, 2021; check current law before relying on a rule.
datasets.attribution: Source: Probative, Eviction laws by state and territory: notice, cure, just cause, fees and timing (LSC), version 2.0.0, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23963453, licensed CC BY 4.0.

datasets.disclaimer: Not legal advice. The file is a research coding of the laws in effect on January 1, 2021, made by the Legal Services Corporation and Temple University from statutes, regulations and court rules. Laws change and local rules can differ; confirm the current rule in the official code before relying on it. Prepared for research and marketing planning.

datasets.title: Eviction filings by county and year (LSC Civil Court Data Initiative)
datasets.summary: Eviction filings (cases) by county and month from the Legal Services Corporation's Civil Court Data Initiative Eviction Tracker, which collects residential eviction filings from state and local courts: 1,464 counties and 34 states and territories, January 2016 through September 2025. Each record carries the filings of every full calendar year the county reports, the last twelve months where all twelve are present, filings per 100 renter households, the poverty rate and the latest month against the county's own historical average. Counties carry the Census FIPS code. LSC's data are released under CC0 1.0. The states and territories in the file are the ones LSC reports; the US record totals a year or month only where every one of them reports it.
datasets.uses: Use it to size landlord-tenant and housing-defense work in the counties a firm serves: how many eviction cases are filed there, how that has moved over the years and through the pandemic, and how filings compare with the number of renter households. Agents can look up a state and its counties, compare up to ten states, or search a county by name.

datasets.disclaimer: Not legal advice. These are counts of eviction cases filed in court, kept for research and market sizing. A filing is not an eviction carried out, a finding against a tenant or a measure of need, and one household can be filed against more than once. Questions about an eviction are for a licensed attorney or a local legal aid office.

HUD's list is one row per filed case; only counts are kept. A case can cite several bases, so the bases add up to more than the cases.
datasets.uses: Use it to see where fair housing complaints are filed, which bases they cite (disability and race lead) and how filings changed from 2006 to 2020, as context for housing-discrimination and civil-rights work. Agents can look up a state or county, compare several, or search by basis ("disability", "familial status"). The file ends on June 30, 2020.

datasets.title: Fatal crashes by county and type: trucks, motorcycles, pedestrians and bicyclists, NHTSA FARS 2019 to 2024
datasets.summary: Fatal motor-vehicle crashes in every US county, state and the nation for 2019 to 2024, from the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration's Fatality Analysis Reporting System (FARS). One record per county, state and the US: fatal crashes and deaths in the newest year, the crashes that involved a large truck, a motorcycle, a pedestrian or a bicyclist, the pedestrians, bicyclists and motorcyclists killed, alcohol-impaired, speeding and work-zone crashes, rural and urban roads, deaths per 100,000 residents, and every earlier year. Every county-year equals the accident table's own rows, and the counties add up to the state and the state to the nation. 2019 to 2023 are NHTSA's final files; 2024 is its first (annual report) release. The county-by-year table is at /research/fatal-crashes-by-county/data.csv. Counts only.

datasets.title: Federal civil cases filed, by county of the plaintiff's residence, case type and year (Federal Judicial Center)
datasets.summary: How many federal civil lawsuits are filed in each U.S. county, and of what kind, over the last ten complete federal fiscal years, from the Federal Judicial Center's Integrated Database (IDB). A case is counted in the county where the first-listed plaintiff lives (the first-listed defendant's county when the United States sues; the tract's county in land condemnation cases), by 16 nature-of-suit groups plus multidistrict litigations (MDLs), and rolled up to Probative's practice areas. One record per county carries all ten years, the prior-year change and the year-by-year history. Cases that cannot be placed in a county are published as rows of their own, per state and nationally: plaintiffs who live in the U.S. outside the court's state (with the MDL share), plaintiffs who live abroad, cases under a retired county code, and cases with an unrecorded county; district records add the same parts for each of the 94 district courts. Every state equals the sum of its counties and these rows, and the national total ties to the U.S. Courts' Table C-2 within a fraction of a percent. Only counts are published: no party, docket number or judge.
datasets.uses: Use it to see where federal civil litigation comes from: which counties send the most injury, employment, civil rights, consumer or Social Security cases to federal court, and how that moves year to year. County means where the plaintiff lives, not where the case is heard, so a county with no federal courthouse still has cases. Read the out-of-state, outside-U.S. and retired-code rows before comparing a state or district: in some years one mass-tort docket makes up most of the out-of-state cases. These are federal filings only, and state courts hear most lawsuits.
datasets.attribution: Source: Probative, Federal civil cases filed, by county of the plaintiff's residence, case type and year (Federal Judicial Center), version 2.0.0, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23963548, licensed CC BY 4.0.

datasets.citeAs: Probative Growth, Federal civil cases filed, by county of the plaintiff's residence, case type and year (Federal Judicial Center), 2026, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23963548
datasets.disclaimer: Not legal advice. These are counts of federal civil case filings from court records, kept for research and marketing planning. A filing says where a plaintiff lives and what kind of case was brought, not that a claim has merit, that a lawyer was hired or how a case ended. County means the county of residence of the first-listed plaintiff (the first-listed defendant's county when the United States sues; the tract's county in land condemnation cases), as the Federal Judicial Center codes it; the court also has codes for a plaintiff who lives in the U.S. outside the court's state and for one who lives abroad. Rights and deadlines in a matter are for your own counsel.

datasets.mcpLine: Federal civil cases filed by plaintiff county, state, district and case type, ten years, with out-of-state totals.
datasets.measurementTechnique: The Federal Judicial Center's civil Integrated Database file (cv88on) is streamed and counted in memory by machine: cases filed per federal fiscal year (October to September, by filing date), per COUNTY code (the county of residence of the first-listed plaintiff), per nature-of-suit code, with cases that carry a multidistrict litigation docket number counted as their own group. County codes are matched to the shared county list; a retired code with one successor goes to that county, one with several is shown as a former county, codes in no list as unrecorded, and codes 88888 and 99999 as out of state and outside the U.S. Nature-of-suit codes are grouped and rolled up to practice areas through the crosswalks. No party name, docket number or judge is read. The totals gate re-adds every state from its counties and these rows, and the U.S. Courts' Table C-2 (national) and Table C-3 (by district) are the second sources.

datasets.title: The US legal market in numbers: headline findings from Probative's open datasets

datasets.uses: Use it to quote a headline figure about the legal market with its source. Look up a finding by its number (F01, F02 and so on) for the sentence, the value, the denominator and the limits, or search the findings by topic. datasets.title: US law firm websites: practices, Spanish, intake, by state, county and practice area
datasets.summary: US law firms, state by state and county by county, from two kinds of open source: law firms' own public websites, read at a slow, spaced rate each week (a few pages per firm), and official state registries published as open data for reuse (New York's attorney registrations and business entities, and the business registries of Colorado, Oregon, Connecticut, Texas and Pennsylvania). For each state, county and practice area we count the firms found, how many have a website we read, and, of those websites, the shares that show Spanish-language pages, a 24/7 intake statement, a free consultation or no fee unless they win, a chat or online booking tool, legal structured data (schema.org LegalService or Attorney), review markup or an llms.txt file, with the median number of pages a firm has about the practice. Every row gives two coverage measures: the firms found against the employer law offices the Census Bureau's County Business Patterns counts, and the websites read against our estimate of the law firms with a website. A state is called a census only when the first reaches 0.70; until then the rows are a sample. These counts are CC BY 4.0. The firm-level rows behind them (name as the firm or registry gives it, offices by county and the yes-or-no facts, each linked to the page it was read on with the date) are published separately under the Open Database License (ODbL) 1.0, because the list of sites comes partly from OpenStreetMap (© OpenStreetMap contributors), and are shown on the /firms/ pages. No firm is rated, scored or ranked, and no individual lawyer's data is published. Website sources: Common Crawl (its web graph and the Web Data Commons structured-data extract), OpenStreetMap and Wikidata.
datasets.uses: Use it to see the supply side of a local legal market next to its demand: how many firms in a county advertise divorce, immigration or car-accident work, and how many of their websites offer Spanish pages or say they answer around the clock. Read the two coverage measures first: where they are low, compare shares rather than totals. Look up a state for its county and practice rows, compare up to ten states, or search for a county or a practice. Firm-by-firm facts are on the /firms/ pages and in the ODbL downloads.

datasets.citeAs: Probative Growth, US law firm websites: practices, Spanish, intake, by state, county and practice area, 2026, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23898107
datasets.disclaimer: Not legal advice. These are counts of facts read from law firms' own public websites and from official open registries on the dates shown, kept for research and marketing planning. Each row's two coverage measures say how much of the market it reaches. The counts describe what websites and registries say, not the quality of any firm or lawyer. A firm can ask us to correct its row or to be left out through the data corrections page; we act within 7 days.

datasets.measurementTechnique: Website firms: candidate sites from Common Crawl's web graph (registered domains with a law-firm term, five recent quarterly graphs, deduplicated), the Web Data Commons schema.org extract of Common Crawl, OpenStreetMap and Wikidata; a crawler reads each site (the crawl-delay a site states is kept, with a 5-second floor per site, one request at a time per site, at most 11 requests per firm and 2 for a site that is not a US law firm; descriptive user agent; no logins, forms, JavaScript or challenge pages; a 403, 429 or challenge page ends the visit) and extracts facts by fixed rules. Registry firms: law-firm entities (names carrying a law-firm signal, active status) from state open-data portals read through their open APIs, matched to website firms by name and ZIP code. Offices are placed in counties with HUD's USPS ZIP-county crosswalk. Every count is re-derived from the firm rows in the release check; a re-crawl of 50 firms measures agreement; coverage (b) compares firms found with Census County Business Patterns 2023 employer law offices (NAICS 541110), coverage (a) compares websites read with a capture-recapture estimate of firm websites (OpenStreetMap vs Common Crawl lists).

datasets.title: Flood insurance claims by county and year (FEMA NFIP, OpenFEMA), 1978 to 2026
datasets.summary: Every National Flood Insurance Program claim in FEMA's public NFIP claims file, counted for the nation, each state and territory and each county by the year of the loss: claims, claims with a payment and dollars paid (building, contents and increased cost of compliance), over all years since 1978, the ten full years 2016 to 2025, the latest full year and the current, partial year, with the flood event that brought the most claims since 2016 in each state. Counts and sums only; no policy, address or claimant detail is kept.
datasets.uses: Use it to size flood and property insurance claim work where it happens: which counties file the most flood claims, how much the program pays there, which storms drove them and how recent years compare with the long record, as context for insurance-claim disputes, bad-faith and property-damage practices. Agents can look up a state and its counties, compare states, or search by county, year or storm name.

This product uses the Federal Emergency Management Agency’s OpenFEMA API, but is not endorsed by FEMA. datasets.measurementTechnique: FEMA publishes every NFIP claim since 1978 through the OpenFEMA API, without policyholder details, refreshed about monthly. The selected fields (state, county code, year and date of loss, amounts paid, flood event) of all claims are read one page at a time at FEMA's crawl-delay and summed by state, county and year of loss. A gate ties the row count to FEMA's own record count for the file, checks that every claim id appears once, re-asks the API for each state's claim count and re-derives 50 random records from the cached pages.

datasets.title: New green cards (lawful permanent residents) by county, country of birth and class of admission
datasets.summary: New lawful permanent residents (green card holders) in the 200 U.S. counties with the most, for the two latest fiscal years: admissions by class (immediate relatives, family preference, employment preference, diversity, refugee and asylee adjustments, other) and the ten countries of birth with the most, with state sums set against the Yearbook of Immigration Statistics state totals. Read from the Department of Homeland Security's county workbooks, in which every cell is rounded to the nearest 10; sums are of rounded cells and understate the true figures, and the share of each state's total they cover is given.
datasets.uses: Use it to see where new permanent residents settle and from where: which counties receive the most green card holders, whether they come through family, employment, diversity or humanitarian routes, and which countries of birth lead. An immigration practice can size family-based, employment-based and naturalization demand by county. Pair it with the legal-need and uscis-offices datasets by state or county FIPS code. Agents can look up a state and its listed counties, compare up to ten states, or search a county by name.

datasets.summary: Federal civil cases from the Federal Judicial Center's Integrated Database (IDB), counted by district, nature-of-suit group and fiscal year: cases filed, the share alleging a class action, the share with a pro se plaintiff, cases terminated, the median days from filing to disposition, the trial share, the median days to trial, and how terminated cases ended (settled, voluntarily dismissed, dismissed, default or consent, motion, trial, other, moved out). Only aggregates are published: no case-level row, party, docket number or judge. Filings re-add to the U.S. Courts' own totals within half a percent.
datasets.uses: Compare how quickly one district disposes of a type of civil case with the rest of the country, or how often a type of suit is filed as a class action or without a lawyer. These are court-wide medians for groups of cases; one case can take far longer or shorter.

datasets.title: Immigration court backlog, representation and asylum outcomes (EOIR workload statistics and case data)
datasets.summary: The size and movement of the U.S. immigration court backlog, from the Executive Office for Immigration Review (EOIR). National series from EOIR's workload and adjudication statistics: pending cases, new cases, completions, the share of completed cases with a representative on record, asylum decisions and the share of grants among grants and denials, asylum applications pending and pending cases of unaccompanied children, by fiscal year. Pending proceedings by immigration court, by the respondent's state of address and by nationality, counted from EOIR's monthly FOIA case-data file, with the share that has a representative of record. Counts only: no case row, name or address is published, and every count published is 11 or more. Every national table is re-added against its own totals row; the case-data counts are shown beside the published totals and never spliced into them.
datasets.uses: Use it to put the immigration court backlog and its representation rate on the record before you plan marketing, intake or staffing in a state. Look up US for the national series, or a two-letter state code for the pending proceedings of respondents with an address there and the immigration courts located in the state. EOIR says its statistics are subject to change, and the case-data counts are not the published backlog total, so quote the national series for the backlog and the case-data counts for where it sits.

datasets.title: Spanish-speaking demand vs Spanish-speaking lawyer supply, by state and metro
datasets.summary: How many people speak Spanish at home in the US, each state and DC, and the metro areas, how many of them speak English less than very well, and how many there are for each lawyer who speaks Spanish at home. Computed from the Census Bureau's American Community Survey (2020 to 2024 five-year tables and microdata), each figure with its 90% margin of error and a reliability grade. Aggregates only: no lawyer or firm is listed or ranked.
datasets.uses: Use it to decide where Spanish-language marketing is worth the effort. Look up your state or metro: the record gives how many residents speak Spanish at home and speak English less than very well, how many lawyers and judges speak Spanish at home, and the ratio between them, each with its margin of error. Pair it with your own intake: if Spanish callers already reach you, the gap in your area tells you how much more demand is waiting. For intake staffing, compare the gap in a metro with the bilingual staff you already have: where Spanish-dominant residents far outnumber Spanish-speaking lawyers, a Spanish-answered phone line and Spanish landing pages tend to be the first fix, before any extra ad spend.

datasets.title: Law firm size, solos and receipts, by state: Census SUSB 2022, Nonemployer Statistics 2024 and Economic Census 2022
datasets.summary: How big U.S. law firms are and what they take in, for the US, every state and DC, from three Census Bureau sources. Employer law firms (NAICS 541110, offices of lawyers) by number of employees (fewer than 5, 5 to 9, 10 to 19, 20 to 99, 100 to 499, 500 or more) with their employees, payroll and receipts, from the Statistics of U.S. Businesses (SUSB) 2022. Businesses with no employees (mostly sole practitioners) and their receipts, by legal form, from Nonemployer Statistics 2024, which publishes legal services (NAICS 5411) as one group. Firm counts, receipts, the share of receipts held by the largest firms and firms by receipts size from the Economic Census 2022. One record per jurisdiction and class. Every size-class row the Census Bureau publishes adds up to its total row, and every figure is the Bureau's own, never estimated.
datasets.uses: Use it to see how many law firms in a state are small, how much they take in, and how many solo practitioners sit outside the employer counts, before you plan marketing for a solo or small firm. Look up your state: the records give each size class with its share of firms and of receipts, the solo (nonemployer) count and receipts per solo, and the Economic Census cross-check. The sources cover different years (2022, 2024, 2022), and a firm with offices in several states is counted in each, so compare shares within a state or the US, not state counts added together.

datasets.title: Lawyer, paralegal and legal-staff pay by state and metro (BLS OEWS)
datasets.summary: How many lawyers, paralegals and legal assistants work in the US, in each state and DC, and in the larger metro areas, and what they are paid: the mean annual wage, the median and the 10th, 25th, 75th and 90th percentile wages, from the Bureau of Labor Statistics' Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics (OEWS) survey, May 2025. Every figure carries its BLS series id and is the one BLS publishes. OEWS counts employees only, not owners, partners or the self-employed, so it is not what a firm's owners earn.
datasets.uses: Use it to price a hire or an in-house team against the local market, or to see where legal staff are paid most. Look up your state or metro: each record gives the employment and the mean annual wage for lawyers and for paralegals and legal assistants (and, for the US and states, legal secretaries and judicial law clerks), so you can compare staff cost with lawyer pay in the same place. When opening a second office, set the two metros side by side: the paralegal wage shows what intake and case-support staff will cost there, and the lawyer wage shows what a lateral hire expects, so the staffing line of the budget comes from the local market rather than from your home city.

datasets.title: Legal marketing and intake hiring demand: pay, headcount and openings (Bureau of Labor Statistics)
datasets.summary: What the roles around a law firm's growth work pay and how many people hold them, and how hiring is moving. Annual pay bands and headcounts (10th, 25th, median, 75th and 90th percentile and mean annual wage) for marketing managers, marketing and market-research specialists, public relations specialists, writers, web designers, web developers, receptionists and customer service representatives from the Bureau of Labor Statistics' Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics (OEWS): nationally within legal services, nationally across all industries, and in every state and DC. Monthly series add legal services employment and average hourly earnings, job openings, hires and quits in professional and business services, and each state's average job-openings and hires rates over the latest year for all nonfarm employers. Aggregates only: no firm, job posting or person.
datasets.uses: Use it to size and price the marketing, web and client-intake hiring a law firm competes for: what a marketing manager or intake receptionist is paid in legal services against all industries and in your state, how many people hold the role, and whether professional-services hiring is heating up or cooling. Agents can look up a place, compare several places, or search by role name.
datasets.attribution: Source: Probative, Legal marketing and intake hiring demand: pay, headcount and openings (Bureau of Labor Statistics), version 1.0.1, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23957260, licensed CC BY 4.0.

datasets.disclaimer: Not legal advice. These are survey estimates from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. OEWS counts employees only and is rounded by the bureau; the monthly series are seasonally adjusted and revised; the state rates cover all nonfarm employers in a state, not only law firms. Pay is a statistic for a group of workers, not an offer or a guide to what one firm should pay.

datasets.measurementTechnique: The annual pay records are read from the statistics bureau's public data API, one series per role, place and measure (OEWS, May reference month), and kept as published; a role-place cell with too few employees, or without a median, is left out of every file. The monthly series are re-read twice a month. A gate re-reads the saved cells, checks that wage bands rise from the 10th to the 90th percentile, that state headcounts do not exceed the national total, that the monthly averages equal their months, and re-queries the API.

datasets.title: Legal need by county: who may need a lawyer, from the American Community Survey
datasets.summary: The people in every U.S. county who may need a lawyer, counted from the Census Bureau's American Community Survey 2020 to 2024 5-year estimates: residents aged 65 and over (and 75 and over and 85 and over), people aged 65 or over living alone and those below the poverty level, residents who are not U.S. citizens, foreign-born residents who arrived since 2010, residents who speak English less than very well (and Spanish speakers among them), divorced residents (and, for states, people divorced in the last year), veterans and veterans with a VA disability rating, residents with a disability, households on SSI, renter households and renters paying 30 or 50 percent of income on rent, residents without health insurance, workers who drive to work and median household income. One record per county (3,144, in the 50 states and DC), per state and for the US, each measure with its 90% margin of error and its share of the population it is counted in.
datasets.uses: Use it as the denominator of a local market: how many people in a county could need an immigration, family, elder-law, estate-planning, veterans' disability, Social Security disability, landlord-tenant or injury lawyer, and how that compares with the state. Pair it with the law-offices, deserts, fatal-crashes or immigration-courts datasets by county FIPS code. Agents can look up a state's counties, compare states, or search a county by name and measure.

datasets.disclaimer: Not legal advice. These are survey estimates of people with a characteristic, not counts of legal problems or cases: a renter, a veteran or a noncitizen does not necessarily need a lawyer. Each estimate has a margin of error, and small counties' estimates are rough.

datasets.summary: Month by month since 2017, what consumers pay for legal services (Consumer Price Index), what law offices receive for their work (Producer Price Index for offices of lawyers, overall and by type of work), and how many people work in legal services (Current Employment Statistics), each next to the all-items or services index where that helps. Every value is read from the Bureau of Labor Statistics' own database with its series id, base period, and a preliminary flag while BLS may still revise it. The consumer index measures a basket item, not a law firm's billing rate. Counts and index values only.
datasets.uses: Use it to put a fee, a billing rate or a hiring plan against the official price record. Look up the consumer legal-services index, the producer price index for offices of lawyers, or legal-services employment; each series comes with its last 24 months and the year-over-year change. To adjust a fee from an earlier year to today's prices, use the legal inflation calculator. To test a fee you set years ago, read the consumer legal-services index for the month you set it and for the latest month: the ratio shows how far legal prices moved in between, and the producer series for law offices shows whether firms' billings moved faster or slower than what clients paid.

datasets.title: Statutes of limitations by state: personal injury, medical malpractice, wrongful death, product liability and property damage
datasets.summary: The filing deadline the statute sets for five kinds of civil claims in every US state and DC: personal injury, medical malpractice, wrongful death, product liability and property damage. Each record gives the period in the statute's own words, the citation, a link to the state's official code site, a verbatim quote, and the date read; where the same text says so, it adds whether the period runs from discovery and any outer limit (statute of repose). Some cells come from a court opinion that quotes or applies the statute; they are marked S (secondary) and name the court, case and date. No calculator and no deadline arithmetic: tolling and exceptions apply.
datasets.uses: Look up one state and claim type, then read the quoted statute and its exceptions before relying on it. For marketing pages and intake scripts that mention filing deadlines, cite the statute and link the official text, never a bare number.
datasets.attribution: Source: Probative, Statutes of limitations by state: personal injury, medical malpractice, wrongful death, product liability and property damage, version 2.0.0, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23963806, licensed CC BY 4.0.

datasets.citeAs: Probative Growth, Statutes of limitations by state: personal injury, medical malpractice, wrongful death, product liability and property damage, 2026, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23963806
datasets.disclaimer: Not legal advice. These are the periods as each statute states them, read in the official code on the date shown. Tolling, discovery rules, notice-of-claim deadlines for claims against a government, minors' rules and other exceptions can shorten or lengthen the time to file, and statutes change. Check the statute and ask a lawyer licensed in the state before relying on a deadline.

datasets.title: Marriage and divorce rates by state (CDC NCHS), 1990 to 2024
datasets.summary: Divorce rates (divorces and annulments per 1,000 residents, by state of occurrence) and marriage rates for every state that reports them to the CDC's National Center for Health Statistics, for 1990, 1995 and each year 2000 to 2024, with each reporting state's latest rate, its 2019 rate and its rate in 2000 (or its first reported year after 2000) and the change since; and the national provisional counts of divorces and marriages each year since 2000, with the states the national divorce count leaves out. Rates and counts only, as NCHS publishes them.
datasets.uses: Use it to size divorce and family-law demand by state: where divorce is most common per resident, how fast it has fallen since 2000 and how many divorces happen nationally each year, beside the divorced residents and county detail in the legal-need dataset. datasets.title: Mass-tort docket tracker, federal MDL pending actions by month since 2019
datasets.summary: Pending actions in every federal multidistrict litigation (MDL), from the Judicial Panel on Multidistrict Litigation's monthly 'Pending MDL Dockets by Actions Pending' reports. One record per docket: the court's docket title, the transferee district, the docket type, actions now pending, actions ever filed, the change over 12 months, the peak pending count, and the docket's monthly pending count since 2019. Version 1.1 adds the 14 MDLs the court closed between 2026-01-01 and 2026-10-01 (dateClosed set, the peak and last count from the monthly series) and the court's reports by district and by docket type, with monthly groupings of the series. Every report's rows add up exactly to the court's own totals row. The full monthly series, judge included, is at /data/v1/mdl/history/index.json (one CSV per year); the district, type and closed-MDL files are at /data/v1/mdl/reports/index.json. Counts and dates only.

datasets.title: Mine accidents, injuries and illnesses by state, county and degree of injury (MSHA), 2000 to 2026

datasets.measurementTechnique: MSHA publishes every reported accident, injury and illness since 2000 as a text file updated weekly, and the mine register with each mine's state and county. datasets.title: Mortgage delinquency by county and state (CFPB Mortgage Performance Trends), monthly from 2008
datasets.summary: The share of mortgages 90 or more days delinquent and 30 to 89 days delinquent, from the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's Mortgage Performance Trends, for the nation, every state and DC and each county the CFPB publishes (counties with at least 1,000 mortgages in its sample): the latest month, the same month a year earlier, the change in percentage points, the highest and lowest 90-day share since January 2008 and each year's December values. Percents only, as the CFPB publishes them.
datasets.uses: Use it to see where homeowners are falling behind on their mortgages, the stage before foreclosure: which states and counties have the highest share of mortgages 90 or more days late, whether it is rising, and how today compares with the 2010 peak, as context for foreclosure-defense, consumer-bankruptcy and real-estate work. Agents can look up a state and its counties, compare states, or search by county name or FIPS code.
datasets.attribution: Source: Probative, Mortgage delinquency by county and state (CFPB Mortgage Performance Trends), monthly from 2008, version 1.0.0, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23845905, licensed CC BY 4.0.

datasets.disclaimer: Not legal advice. These are shares of mortgages in the CFPB's sample that were behind on payments, not counts of foreclosure filings or of people. A delinquent mortgage may be cured, modified or paid off. County figures exist only where the CFPB's sample holds at least 1,000 mortgages.

datasets.title: Noncitizen population by state and county (Census ACS, table B05001)
datasets.summary: How many residents of each state, DC and county are not U.S. citizens, with the margin of error and the share of the population, from the Census Bureau's American Community Survey 5-year estimates (2020-2024), table B05001 (nativity and citizenship status). Each record also splits the citizens into born in the US, born in a U.S. territory, born abroad of American parents and naturalized. These are survey estimates of residents, not of legal status: the table does not separate lawful permanent residents, visa holders or anyone else.
datasets.uses: Use it to size the noncitizen resident population of a market, for example to plan immigration-law or consumer-protection outreach in a county or to compare states. Look up a state: you get the state row and every county in it, each with the estimate, its margin of error and the share of residents. Small counties carry wide margins of error, so compare ranges, not single figures.

datasets.disclaimer: Not legal advice. These are Census Bureau survey estimates for planning. The table counts residents who are not U.S. citizens; it does not measure immigration or legal status.

datasets.title: Nursing home fines and harm citations by county: CMS penalties, actual-harm, immediate-jeopardy and abuse citations
datasets.summary: For every US county with a Medicare- or Medicaid-certified nursing home, every state and territory, and the US: how many certified nursing homes and beds there are, how many times the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) fined them in the last three years and for how many dollars, how often and for how many days it denied payment, and how many health citations inspectors wrote at the actual-harm level or worse (scope and severity G to L), at the immediate-jeopardy level (J to L) and under the abuse, neglect and exploitation tags (F600 to F610), plus the share of rated homes with one star overall. Built each month from the four CMS Provider Data Catalog files behind Care Compare. Counts only: no facility names, addresses or certification numbers, and no resident data (CMS publishes none).
datasets.uses: Use it to size the market for nursing home abuse and neglect cases county by county: where the homes and beds are, where CMS has fined homes and how much, and where inspectors found residents harmed or in immediate jeopardy. A county with many beds, large fines and a high share of one-star homes is where families are most likely to be looking for help. Read it beside the elder population and law-office counts before you decide where to advertise or open an office.
datasets.attribution: Source: Probative, Nursing home fines and harm citations by county: CMS penalties, actual-harm, immediate-jeopardy and abuse citations, version 2.0.0, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23964018, licensed CC BY 4.0.

datasets.citeAs: Probative Growth, Nursing home fines and harm citations by county: CMS penalties, actual-harm, immediate-jeopardy and abuse citations, 2026, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23964018
datasets.disclaimer: Not legal advice. This is a count of public CMS inspection and penalty records, kept for marketing planning. A citation is an inspector's finding, not a court's; a fine can be reduced or withdrawn on appeal; and nothing here says any home or person did anything unlawful.
