datasets.measurementTechnique: Each certified nursing home in the CMS Provider Information file is placed in the county CMS lists for it (matched by name and state to the vintage 2025 county FIPS codes in the crosswalks dataset); its fines and payment denials from the Penalties file and its health citations from the Health Deficiencies file are added to that county, its state and the US. Harm is scope and severity G to L, immediate jeopardy J to L, abuse the federal tags F600 to F610. Totals are checked against the raw files by state and against CMS's own state and national averages.

datasets.title: Attorneys registered with the New York courts, by county, status and year of admission (NYS Office of Court Administration)
datasets.summary: How many lawyers are on New York's official attorney registration list, county by county. For each of the 62 counties the file counts the attorneys whose office address is there by registration status (currently registered, inside the 30-day reregistration window, delinquent, resigned, deceased, disbarred or suspended, incapacitated), by decade of admission to the New York bar, and per 10,000 residents using the Census Bureau's county population estimate. Further records count registrations with an office in each other state or territory, registrations with no office address in the public file, and the four judicial departments of admission, and the state record carries the admission-year history. Only counts are published: no name, address, phone number, firm or registration number is read, because the pull asks the court's open data portal for server-side totals and never downloads rows. Counts in a disciplinary status or an admission decade are published from five up. Every record adds up to the state, the state ties to the source's own row count, and the American Bar Association's 2025 count of New York resident active lawyers sits between the two bounds the file allows.
datasets.uses: Use it to see how many lawyers already serve a New York county before choosing where to advertise: active attorneys per 10,000 residents, how many are newly admitted, and how many are no longer in practice (delinquent, resigned, deceased). A county here is where the attorney's office is, not where clients live, and a lawyer in New York City may serve clients across the state. More than a quarter of the active attorneys have no office address in the public file and another quarter list an office outside New York, so county totals count lawyers with a published New York office, not every New York license.

datasets.summary: Workers' compensation claims assembled by the New York State Workers' Compensation Board in every New York county, for each accident year from 2000: the number of claims, how many have an attorney or representative (count and share), how many are controverted, how many have had a hearing and how many hearings were held, and how many are classified permanent partial or permanent total disability or occupational disease. datasets.uses: Use it to size the workers' compensation market in New York county by county: how many claims are assembled each year, how often injured workers are represented (a measure of how much of the market lawyers already serve), how many claims are fought, and how many reach hearings and permanent disability. Pair it with the work-injuries and law-offices datasets by county FIPS code. Agents can look up New York, compare years, or search a county by name.

datasets.title: Legal-marketing ethics opinions, 2004–2026
datasets.summary: An index of US state and ABA ethics opinions, committee guidelines and court rulings on lawyer advertising and marketing, from 2004 to 2026 (most from 2015 on, plus earlier landmarks): lead generators, pay-per-lead, reviews, testimonials, trade names, websites, social media, chatbots and AI tools, competitor keywords and more. Version 1.1 adds an AI sub-index: 14 AI opinions coded on six marketing questions (chatbot disclosure, AI-made ads, intake and solicitation, superiority claims, confidentiality in marketing tools, and fees). Each record gives the issuing body, number, date, topics, a one-sentence holding in our words, a practical step, whether it is still in force, the official link, an exact short quote and the date read. It is not the opinions' full text.
datasets.uses: Use it before you try a new kind of marketing. If you want to buy leads, pay a referral platform, quote a client review, run a chatbot or bid on a rival firm's name, search the index for that topic and your state first. You will see which committees have already answered the question, what they said in plain words, what step it points to, and whether the answer still stands. Then read the opinion itself through its official link before you rely on it. Typical questions it answers: can a firm pay a lead generator per lead or per signed case; may an ad quote a client's online review; may a firm buy a competitor's name as a search keyword; who is responsible when a chatbot on the firm's site answers a legal question; and whether a trade name or a website domain can imply a specialty. Each answer names the committee or court, the opinion number and its date, so a partner can hand the citation straight to counsel. Version 1.1 also answers a newer question: what has each bar said about AI in marketing? Filter to the topic "ai" to see the 14 AI opinions, and read the six coded fields to see which ones say anything about chatbots, AI-made ads, intake, superiority claims, confidentiality and fees.

datasets.title: Legal ad-platform policy tracker
datasets.summary: The ad-platform policies that affect US law-firm advertising on Google Ads, Google Local Services, YouTube, Microsoft Ads, Meta, LinkedIn and ChatGPT ads: what each rule says in plain English, what a firm should do about it, which practice areas it touches, when it took effect, and a dated log of changes. Each record quotes the platform's own policy or help page and gives the date it was read.
datasets.uses: Use it before a campaign goes live, or when an ad is suddenly disapproved. Look up the platform and your practice area: the record says what the policy asks in plain English, what to change in your account or your ads, and the date the rule began. The change log shows what moved since you last checked, so a rejection is easier to trace to the rule behind it. Every record links to the platform's own page, which is the wording that counts. Typical questions it answers: what Google Local Services Ads checks before the 'Google Verified' badge shows; which legal services need Google's legal-services certification; what Meta allows for lead forms and special ad categories; how Microsoft Advertising treats bail bonds or debt relief; and what the newer ChatGPT and AI-answer ad programs say about legal advertisers. Each record says which practice areas it touches, so a family-law or immigration firm can skip the rules that only bind injury firms.

datasets.title: Deaths, births, migration and older residents by county (Census population estimates), 2020 to 2025
datasets.summary: The Census Bureau's population estimates for every U.S. county, every state and DC and the nation: deaths, births, international migration and domestic migration in the year to July 1, 2025 and summed over the five years since July 1, 2020, with the Bureau's own rates per 1,000 residents; residents on July 1, 2025 and on the April 1, 2020 estimates base; and residents aged 65 and over, 75 and over and 85 and over, with their share of all residents and the growth of the 65-and-over population since 2020. Counts only, from the Bureau's public Vintage 2025 files.
datasets.uses: Use it to size estate-planning, probate, elder-law and guardianship demand where it is: how many people die each year in a county (the estates that may need administering), how many residents are 75 or 85 and older and how fast the older population is growing; and to see where new residents arrive from abroad or from other counties, as context for immigration and real-estate work. Agents can look up a state and its counties, compare states, or search by county name or FIPS code.
datasets.attribution: Source: Probative, Deaths, births, migration and older residents by county (Census population estimates), 2020 to 2025, version 1.0.0, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23845912, licensed CC BY 4.0.

datasets.disclaimer: Not legal advice. These are Census Bureau estimates built from birth and death records, tax and Medicare files and survey data, not counts of court cases or estates. A death is not a probate filing: many estates pass without one. Rates and shares are for planning, not for any one person's matter.

datasets.measurementTechnique: The Census Bureau publishes, each March, county population totals and components of change (births, deaths, international and domestic migration) and, each June, county population by age. datasets.title: Consumer product recalls by year and hazard (CPSC recall notices)
datasets.summary: Recalls announced by the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) since 2010, counted for the whole period, for each recall year and for each of ten hazard classes (fire and burn, falls and tip-overs, laceration, choking and suffocation, ingestion, entrapment and pinch injuries, electric shock, poisoning and chemicals, crashes and collisions, drowning, plus a class for the rest). Each count comes with the number of recalls whose notice reports an injury and the number that report a death, parsed from the notice's own incident text, and with the units the notices give. A recall that names several hazards counts once in each class and once in the totals. The counts come from CPSC's recall API; no firm names, contacts or narratives are kept.
datasets.uses: Use it to see which product hazards drive recalls, how recall volume changes year to year, and how often a recall notice reports a harm, as context for product-liability work. Agents can read the records at one level (the whole period, each year or each hazard class), compare levels, or search by hazard or year.
datasets.attribution: Source: Probative, Consumer product recalls by year and hazard (CPSC recall notices), version 2.0.0, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23964084, licensed CC BY 4.0.

datasets.citeAs: Probative Growth, Consumer product recalls by year and hazard (CPSC recall notices), 2026, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23964084
datasets.disclaimer: Not legal advice. These are counts of recall notices published by the Consumer Product Safety Commission, kept for research and market sizing. A recall is not a finding that a product caused any harm to any person, and it says nothing about whether anyone has a claim; deadlines for injury claims differ by state. Questions about an injury are for a licensed attorney.

datasets.measurementTechnique: One request per calendar year to CPSC's keyless recall API; each notice is reduced to a parsed row (hazard classes by keyword rules on the notice's hazard text, injury and death flags from its incident text after removing sentences that say none was reported, and the stated unit count), then counted by year and by hazard class. A gate re-fetches 50 random notices live, re-derives the same row and compares, and checks that classes, years and the whole period tie.

datasets.title: Railroad casualties and crossing incidents by county (FRA Forms 55a, 57 and 54)
datasets.summary: Railroad casualties, highway-rail grade crossing incidents and train accidents that railroads reported to the Federal Railroad Administration (FRA), 2021 through July 2026, for 2,315 counties with at least one report, 50 states and the US: 41,307 casualties (5,136 deaths and 36,171 nonfatal injuries or illnesses) from Form 55a, split by who was hurt (railroad employee on duty or off duty, contractor or volunteer, passenger, trespasser, other non-trespasser), 12,345 crossing incidents with the people killed and injured (Form 57) and 14,018 rail equipment accidents (Form 54), with the casualty count of each incident year. FRA's county codes are Census FIPS codes; counties retired since keep their old code. Counts come from FRA's rolling six-year views on data.transportation.gov and are aggregated server-side; no narrative or person-level field is read.
datasets.uses: Use it to size railroad-injury and crossing-accident work in the counties a firm serves: how many railroad employees, passengers, trespassers and motorists were hurt or killed there, how crossing incidents compare with train accidents, and how a county compares with its state. Agents can look up a state and its counties, compare up to ten states, or search a county by name.
datasets.attribution: Source: Probative, Railroad casualties and crossing incidents by county (FRA Forms 55a, 57 and 54), version 2.0.0, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23964086, licensed CC BY 4.0.

datasets.citeAs: Probative Growth, Railroad casualties and crossing incidents by county (FRA Forms 55a, 57 and 54), 2026, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23964086
datasets.disclaimer: Not legal advice. These are counts of events railroads reported to the Federal Railroad Administration, kept for research and market sizing. A report is not a finding of fault, and it says nothing about whether anyone has a claim; a railroad employee's injury claim has its own federal rules and deadlines. Questions about an injury are for a licensed attorney.

datasets.mcpLine: Railroad casualties, crossing incidents and train accidents by county from FRA Forms 55a, 57 and 54, by who was hurt.
datasets.measurementTechnique: Aggregated server-side (SoQL group by state, county, incident year and person class) from three views on data.transportation.gov: Form 55a casualties (bx7m-yn3v), Form 57 highway-rail crossing incidents (uwah-u9bn) and Form 54 rail equipment accidents (jm8x-ccxs). The views cover six calendar years and roll forward: a year that leaves the view stays in the dataset as last read, and years still in the view are re-read every month because railroads can amend their reports for five years. County codes are padded to Census FIPS and checked against the shared crosswalks. A gate checks that the aggregates add up to the views' row counts, that counties add up to states and states to the US, compares every state with FRA's raw Form 55a and Form 57 source tables, and re-counts fifty random county-years from the live view.

datasets.title: Referral-fee and fee-splitting rules for lawyers, by state
datasets.summary: When lawyers in different firms may split a fee, and what a lawyer may pay for a referral, in the US states and DC it covers. Each record gives the state's fee-division rule (ABA Model Rule 1.5(e) or its equivalent: the proportion or joint-responsibility test, how the client must agree, whether each share is disclosed, any cap) and its rule on paying for recommendations (Model Rule 7.2(b) or its equivalent: referral-service charges, reciprocal referral agreements, nominal gifts), each quoted from the official rules text with the date read.
datasets.uses: Look up one state before you agree a co-counsel or referral split, or before you sign with a referral service or lead vendor. Read the quoted rule text, and the state's ethics opinions, before you rely on it: this is a marketing reference, not legal advice.

datasets.title: Unwanted-call and text-message complaints to the FCC, by state and month
datasets.summary: Complaints about unwanted calls, robocalls and telemarketing that people filed with the Federal Communications Commission (FCC), counted by state, month, issue and method (text message, prerecorded voice, live voice and others) from January 2015, with the last 12 months set against the 12 before and per 100,000 residents. One record per state, DC, Puerto Rico and territory for text-message complaints and one for phone-call complaints. The counts come from the FCC's open Consumer Complaints Data, grouped on the FCC's server so no complaint, caller number or free text is ever copied, and the state rows add up to a separate FCC-side count for every month. Complaints are self-reported and unverified, not findings of any violation.
datasets.uses: Use it to see where people report the most unwanted texts and calls, and how that has moved, before you plan texting or phone outreach. Look up your state: the record gives the last 12 months of text-message or phone-call complaints, the rate per 100,000 residents, the change from the 12 months before, and three years of monthly counts. Read the rate as how often people in a state file complaints, not how often calls are made; a few filers can move a small state.
datasets.attribution: Source: Probative, Unwanted-call and text-message complaints to the FCC, by state and month, version 2.0.0, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23964125, licensed CC BY 4.0.

datasets.citeAs: Probative Growth, Unwanted-call and text-message complaints to the FCC, by state and month, 2026, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23964125
datasets.disclaimer: Not legal advice. These are counts of complaints people filed with the FCC, kept for marketing planning. A complaint is a report, not a finding that anyone broke a law, and no phone number or complaint text is published. Texting and calling rules (the TCPA and state laws) are for your own counsel.

datasets.title: Google searches for a lawyer by practice area and state, English and Spanish (Google Ads Keyword Planner, Trends and Autocomplete)
datasets.summary: How many people search Google for a lawyer each month, practice by practice: 84 query families (personal injury and its niches such as truck accidents, mesothelioma and birth injury; immigration subtypes; bankruptcy chapters; estate planning; intellectual property; employment subtypes and more), each asked in the plain English and Spanish words people type. For the whole US, all 50 states and DC, the file gives the searches a month in English and in Spanish (12-month average), the head query of each language and the month-by-month series, from Google Ads Keyword Planner (October 2025 to September 2026). Google reports close variants with one combined figure, so a family total counts each distinct monthly series once, and every query's own figure is listed. A second measured source, a DataForSEO pull of the same Google Ads data for the US and 27 states, is kept as a cross-check: a record per place counts the queries on which the two agree. Free Google sources add, for the head queries with enough data, Google Trends interest by state over the last 12 months (a relative index, never mixed with counts) and the Google Autocomplete suggestions for the head queries whose suggestions pass the filter (only suggestions in which every word is a common word, so no firm, brand, person or place is named). Where our firm census holds 100 or more firm websites for a practice in a state, a ratio gives the searches a month per firm website, with both inputs.
datasets.uses: Use it to size a market before you spend: how many people search for a truck accident or immigration lawyer each month in a state, how much of that is in Spanish, which months are busy, and how many firms already compete for each search. Search counts are Google's own estimates for the 12 months shown and are rounded by Google; read them as orders of magnitude. A family's queries are the common ways to ask; long, local and misspelled searches are not counted, so totals are a floor. Trends figures are indexes (top state = 100), and Autocomplete shows what Google suggests, not how often.
datasets.attribution: Source: Probative, Google searches for a lawyer by practice area and state, English and Spanish (Google Ads Keyword Planner, Trends and Autocomplete), version 1.1.0, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23877019, licensed CC BY 4.0.

datasets.citeAs: Probative Growth, Google searches for a lawyer by practice area and state, English and Spanish (Google Ads Keyword Planner, Trends and Autocomplete), 2026, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23877019

datasets.title: Google search landscape for legal searches: directories, videos, People Also Ask and how concentrated the top 10 is
datasets.summary: What a person sees when they search Google for a lawyer or legal help in the United States: how often lawyer directories (FindLaw, Justia, Avvo, Super Lawyers and others), videos and the People Also Ask box appear, how many of the top-10 results are directories, and how concentrated the results are in a few websites, by practice area, search type (cost, near me, best, versus, how-to) and language (English, Spanish). Built from 2,240 legal searches (22,089 top-10 results) saved from Google on 2026-10-29 and 30; every group has at least 30 searches and no firm or person is named.
datasets.uses: Use it to see in which searches directories appear in the top 10 and which belong to firm sites, videos and forums, so you know where a firm page can rank and where a listing or a video is the way in. A share is the percent of the group's searches (or top-10 results) that show the feature; the row says how many searches it rests on.

datasets.title: State trial-court case filings by county, court level and case type: Texas, Washington, Maryland, Indiana, Wisconsin, Virginia, Pennsylvania, Oregon, West Virginia, Nebraska, Maine, California, Louisiana and Hawaii
datasets.summary: How many cases are filed in state trial courts, by county, court level and case group, from each state court system's own published statistics. Texas (Office of Court Administration): district, constitutional county and statutory county courts, fiscal years 2023–24 and 2024–25, with district-court filings by case type. Washington (Administrative Office of the Courts): superior courts and district and municipal courts (criminal, civil, domestic, probate, juvenile, traffic, DUI, protection orders, small claims), calendar year 2025. Maryland (Judiciary data dashboard): circuit-court filings by case type and District Court filings (landlord-tenant, civil, criminal, DUI, traffic citations, peace orders), fiscal years 2012 to 2025. Indiana (Office of Judicial Administration): circuit and superior court new filings by Rule 8 case type (felony, misdemeanor, tort, collection, small claims, eviction, foreclosure, domestic relations, estates, juvenile), calendar year 2025 (provisional) beside 2024. Wisconsin (Director of State Courts Office): circuit-court cases opened by category, felony to juvenile, 2020 to 2025. Virginia (Office of the Executive Secretary): circuit, general district and juvenile and domestic relations district courts by locality (county or independent city), calendar year 2025. Pennsylvania (Administrative Office of Pennsylvania Courts): courts of common pleas in all 67 counties, civil cases by type (motor-vehicle and other torts, mass torts, malpractice, contract and debt, landlord-tenant, foreclosure) and criminal, protection from abuse, support, custody, divorce, juvenile, adoption and guardianship cases, calendar year 2024. Oregon (Oregon Judicial Department): circuit courts in all 36 counties, calendar year 2025. West Virginia (Supreme Court of Appeals): circuit, family and magistrate courts in all 55 counties, calendar year 2025. Nebraska (Judicial Branch): county and district courts in all 93 counties and the separate juvenile courts of three of them, fiscal year 2024–25. Maine (Judicial Branch): superior courts, unified criminal dockets and district courts in all 16 counties, fiscal years 2021–22 to 2025–26. California (Judicial Council): superior courts in all 58 counties (motor-vehicle and other injury, limited civil, eviction, small claims, felony, misdemeanor, traffic, marital, parentage, domestic violence, child support, juvenile delinquency and dependency, guardianship, other probate, mental health), fiscal year 2024–25. Louisiana (Supreme Court of Louisiana, Judicial Administrator's Office): district courts in 61 of the state's 64 parishes (civil, criminal, traffic and juvenile cases), calendar year 2025 beside 2024 where the 2024 report's row matches. Hawaii (Hawaii State Judiciary): circuit courts in all four circuits, each mapped to its county (motor-vehicle and other injury, contract, foreclosure, probate proceedings, circuit criminal cases), fiscal year 2024–25. Every record keeps the state's own category names and the numbers added into each group (components), and carries a harmonized group and the practice areas it bears on, so a county's filings can be read as demand for personal injury, family, landlord-tenant, small claims and debt, probate, criminal and DUI, juvenile and traffic work. In every source the counties add up to the state's own printed total where it prints one (Texas, Washington, Indiana, Wisconsin, Virginia, Pennsylvania, Oregon, West Virginia, Nebraska, Hawaii), Louisiana's parish records are the parishes whose rows add up to the printed district totals and its state row is the state's printed total, and the state rows for Maryland are the sum of the counties. Every record carries its FIPS code (the state's on a state row, the county's on a county row) so it joins Census and other county data. Counts only: no lawyer or firm is listed or ranked.
datasets.uses: Use it to see where the legal work is, county by county, for the states listed. A case filed is a new case (Texas counts new cases and motions added to the docket), so the counts show how much demand each practice area has in each county; they do not show how many of those people hired a lawyer. Compare a county with its state row and with the year before. Read the court level: the same county can have several levels of court, and one level is not the county's total. The harmonized groups are our grouping of each state's own categories, and the state's category is always shown beside it. Compare a group across states with care: courts differ in what they hear, and in whether they count cases or incidents (Maryland counts traffic citations as incidents).

datasets.measurementTechnique: Texas: the Office of Court Administration's county summary and district activity detail workbooks (Excel) are read by machine and quoted back as printed; a table counts only if the counties add up to the workbook's own statewide Total row in every column and the district Total rows equal the Activity Detail workbook. Other states: each state's published Excel or CSV file is read by machine, the state's categories are mapped to harmonized groups and the practice taxonomy with the original category and every component kept on the record, and a state counts only if its gates pass: Washington counties = the Statewide Total row in all columns, each county's categories = its Total Filings, limited-jurisdiction courts = their county rows = the statewide row; Indiana court rows = the workbook's STATE row in every case-type column and each row's case types = TOTAL; Wisconsin counties = the state's own Caseload Summary row in every category; Virginia: the three caseload PDFs (circuit, general district, juvenile and domestic relations) are read from the PDF text layer page by page, each month row must add to its printed year total, the localities must add to the printed Statewide row in every category and in total, every locality's categories to its printed Locale Total, and each circuit's or district's localities to its printed total; Pennsylvania: the statewide and 67 county caseload PDFs are read from the PDF text layer, in every county and statewide the 46 civil case types must add to the printed total docketed cases and to each of the seven printed section subtotals (all 476 of them, statewide and county), and the 67 counties must add to the statewide report in every civil case type and every new-case count; Oregon: the Cases Filed PDF, where the case types must add to their category and the categories to the printed total in every county, each district's counties to its printed total, and the 36 counties to the statewide table in every row; West Virginia: the annual statistics report's county tables, where the 55 counties must add to the printed Total row in every column; Nebraska: the three fiscal-year 2025 caseload report PDFs (county courts, district courts, separate juvenile courts), where in every judicial district the counties must add to the printed Total row in every column, each row's categories to its printed total and the Total row to the district summary row, and the district rows to the printed Statewide row, and the separate juvenile counties to the printed district table; Maine: the eight region PDFs and the statewide detail PDF, where each court's sections must add to its printed total, the courts must add to each region's printed total, and each case type summed over all courts must equal the statewide detail row (two small rows the state does not explain are noted on the record, and child protective, which the state explains, is noted too); California: the Court Statistics Report's county tables (also the ca-courts dataset, folded in), where the 58 counties must add to the printed Statewide row in every column and in both years where every county reports the year before; Louisiana: the 2025 Annual Report's district-court table, where each parish row must add up (juvenile, civil, criminal and traffic to its printed total), a parish counts only when its judicial district's parish rows add to the printed District Totals row in every column, the 42 District Totals rows must add to the printed Statewide row, each figure of the table is re-read by local OCR from the page image, and the 2024 report's page 34, an image with no text layer, is read by two OCR passes that must agree (a 2024 prior is kept only where the parish's 2024 row adds up and its total equals the 2024 figure the 2025 report prints); Hawaii: the Judiciary's FY2025 statistical supplement, where every circuit-court row must add (the opening caseload plus filed equals the total caseload, the sixteen civil-action types add to Civil Actions) and the four circuits must add to the printed ALL CIRCUITS row; Maryland has no printed total so duplicates, blanks and county coverage are checked and the state row is the county sum. A failed gate writes nothing.

datasets.title: Toxic chemical releases by county (EPA Toxics Release Inventory)
datasets.summary: Toxic chemicals that industrial and federal facilities reported releasing on site to the Environmental Protection Agency's Toxics Release Inventory (TRI) in reporting year 2024, for 2,437 counties with a reporting facility, 56 states and territories and the US: 21,482 facilities and 2,842,308,160 pounds in all (530,322,130 to air, 188,664,266 to water, 2,123,321,764 to land), with the pounds of known or suspected carcinogens, PFAS, ethylene oxide, benzene and lead, and the on-site total of each of the earlier years kept (2020, 2021, 2022, 2023). State records list the three largest parent companies. Counties carry the Census FIPS code. Dioxin-like compounds, which facilities report in grams, are converted to pounds. TRI counts reported releases by listed chemicals from covered facilities; it is not a measure of exposure or of harm.
datasets.uses: Use it to size toxic-exposure and environmental-injury work in the counties a firm serves: how many covered facilities release listed chemicals there, how many pounds, how much of it is carcinogens or PFAS, and how a county compares with its state and with earlier years. Agents can look up a state and its counties, compare up to ten states, or search a county by name.

datasets.disclaimer: Not legal advice. These are pounds that covered facilities reported releasing, kept for research and market sizing. A release is not an exposure, a finding that anyone was harmed or a finding of fault, and the Toxics Release Inventory covers only listed chemicals and facilities above reporting thresholds. Questions about exposure or injury are for a licensed attorney or a health professional.

datasets.measurementTechnique: Read from EPA's TRI Basic Data Files, one per reporting year (data.epa.gov), cached outside the repository; only aggregates are kept: per state and county name, the facilities and the 'ON-SITE RELEASE TOTAL' in pounds by release route (air, water, land) and by chemical tags (known or suspected carcinogens, PFAS, ethylene oxide, benzene, lead and lead compounds). The tags are not a partition: ethylene oxide and benzene are also carcinogens. County names are matched to vintage-2025 FIPS codes in the shared crosswalks (names EPA cuts at 25 characters are completed against the county list). A gate re-reads the whole file with a separate routine, checks that counties add up to states and states to the US, compares six states with EPA's separate per-state TRI files, and re-sums fifty random county-chemical-group cells.

datasets.title: Truck and bus crashes by county, state and year (FMCSA crash file)
datasets.summary: Crashes involving a commercial truck or bus that states reported to the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (FMCSA), counted from its Motor Carrier Management Information System (MCMIS) crash file for every county, state and territory and the US over the last ten complete calendar years. Each record gives, for the latest year, the crashes, the fatal crashes, the crashes with injuries, the crashes where a vehicle was towed away, the crashes involving a bus, the deaths and the injuries, with the whole ten-year history and the ten-year totals. A crash is one state crash report, counted once however many trucks and buses it involved, and its deaths and injuries are counted once. State records add the number of active carriers based in the state, from the FMCSA Company Census File. Counties with no reported crash are listed with zeros, and reports without a usable county code are kept in a 'county not given' row for their state, so counties always add up to the state.
datasets.uses: Use it to size the truck-accident market in the counties a firm serves: how many truck and bus crashes happen there each year, how many are fatal or cause injuries, and whether the count is rising. Look up a state to get every county in it, compare up to ten states, or search for a county by name. It counts only federally reportable crashes, and some states report more completely than others, so read it alongside the fatal-crash census from NHTSA.

datasets.disclaimer: Not legal advice. These are counts of crash reports kept for research and marketing planning. A reported crash says nothing about who was at fault, and the counts leave out crashes that did not meet the federal reporting threshold. Rights and deadlines after a crash are for your own counsel.

datasets.title: Texas employers without workers' compensation coverage (non-subscribers), by county
datasets.summary: Texas does not require most private employers to carry workers' compensation insurance. Employers that opt out file a notice of no coverage (DWC Form-005) with the state each year. This dataset counts those filings from October 2024 to September 2026: for the state, and for each county with at least five non-subscribing employers, the employers with a location in the county, their locations and the filings by year. Counties with fewer than five are combined. Employers are businesses: no company names or addresses are kept. A ZIP code is placed in the county that holds most of its land.
datasets.uses: Use it to see where injured workers in Texas may have no workers' compensation to turn to: which counties have the most employers that opted out, as context for personal-injury and workplace-injury marketing in Texas. Agents can look up the state, compare several counties or search by county name.

datasets.citeAs: Probative Growth, Texas employers without workers' compensation coverage (non-subscribers), by county, 2026, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23964216
datasets.disclaimer: Not legal advice. These are counts of notices that employers filed with the Texas Division of Workers' Compensation. A non-subscribing employer can be sued for its negligence by an injured worker, but whether any claim exists depends on the facts; claims and deadlines are for your own counsel. The count of employers is a floor: not every non-subscriber files, and a filing covers a year.

ZIP codes are placed in counties with the Census 2020 ZCTA-to-county file (the county with most of the ZIP's land), and a ZIP that is not a ZCTA goes to the county of the same city's other ZIPs when they all fall in one county. datasets.title: County and state unemployment: BLS Local Area Unemployment Statistics, annual averages and latest month
datasets.summary: The unemployment rate, number unemployed, employed and labor force for every county and state, from the Bureau of Labor Statistics' Local Area Unemployment Statistics (LAUS) program: the annual average for each year 2015 to 2025 and the latest 13 months. Each county and state record carries the latest annual average, the change from the year before and since 2015, and the latest month (preliminary until BLS revises it). County figures are model-based estimates that BLS controls to its state totals; the build checks that county employment, unemployment and labor force add up to the state's. Alaska appears with its current census-area codes, and Connecticut by its planning regions.
datasets.uses: Use it to see how tight or slack the labor market is in the counties a firm serves, and where it is turning: rising unemployment is the backdrop to layoffs, wage disputes and unemployment-benefit appeals, and a county's rate against its state's shows where local conditions differ. Look up a state to get every county in it, compare up to ten states, or search by county name. These are survey-based model estimates, not a count of people, and the newest month is preliminary.

datasets.summary: Employed wage and salary workers, union members and workers represented by unions (members plus workers covered by a union contract) in every state, DC and the nation, from the Bureau of Labor Statistics' annual Union Members release (Current Population Survey): numbers in thousands as BLS prints them, each as a percent of employed workers, for the latest year and the year before, with the change in the members' percent. The 2025 annual figures average the 11 months BLS published (January to September, November and December).
datasets.uses: Use it to size labor-relations and union-side or employer-side labor work by state: where union membership and contract coverage are highest, how many workers that is, and whether it is rising, beside the EEOC charges and wage-and-hour cases in the employment datasets. Agents can look up a state, compare states, or search by state name.

datasets.title: USCIS naturalization and green card applications by field office
datasets.summary: Applications to U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services for naturalization (Form N-400, general and military) and for a green card by adjustment of status (Form I-485, family, employment, humanitarian and other), received, approved, denied and pending at every USCIS field office and service centre, for each fiscal quarter USCIS has published, with the nationwide totals. Read cell for cell from the agency's quarterly performance workbooks and tied to its service-wide quarterly totals. Every cell is kept as published and never estimated.
datasets.uses: Use it to see where naturalization and green card work is concentrated and where it waits: how many applications each USCIS office takes in, decides and has pending, and how the mix of family, employment and humanitarian green card cases differs by office. An immigration practice can compare the offices that serve its clients. Pair it with the legal-need and immigration-courts datasets by state. Agents can look up a state, compare up to ten states, or search an office by name.

datasets.citeAs: Probative Growth, USCIS naturalization and green card applications by field office, 2026, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23964258
datasets.disclaimer: Not legal advice. These are counts of applications that USCIS received and decided at each office, not the outcome of any one case or a prediction of one: a pending count says how many applications are waiting, not how long yours will wait or where it will be decided. Questions about an immigration case are for a licensed immigration attorney or an accredited representative.

datasets.title: VA disability compensation recipients by county and combined rating
datasets.summary: Veterans receiving VA disability compensation in every U.S. county on September 30, 2025 (fiscal year 2025), from the Department of Veterans Affairs county file on data.va.gov: the total and the count in each combined service-connected rating band (0 to 20%, 30 to 40%, 50 to 60%, 70 to 90% and 100%), by age group (17 to 44, 45 to 64, 65 and over) and by sex, with the same county's total and 100% count a year earlier. One record per county (3,144, in the 50 states and DC), per state and DC (the sum of its counties), for Puerto Rico, for the other territories, for veterans paid abroad, for unknown addresses and for the US. Every figure is one VA publishes; none is estimated.
datasets.uses: Use it to size a veterans' disability practice in the counties a firm serves: how many veterans already receive compensation there, how many have a low or middle rating and how many are already rated fully disabled, how fast the count is growing, and how a county compares with its state. Pair it with the law-offices or deserts datasets by county FIPS code. Agents can look up a state and its counties, compare up to ten states, or search a county by name.

datasets.citeAs: Probative Growth, VA disability compensation recipients by county and combined rating, 2026, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23898138
datasets.disclaimer: Not legal advice. These are counts of veterans already receiving VA disability compensation, not claims, appeals or unmet need: a rating says how VA scored a service-connected condition, not whether a veteran needs a lawyer or could get a higher rating. Questions about a claim are for an accredited attorney, agent or veterans service officer.

datasets.title: VA disability compensation, pension and survivor dollars by county (VA GDX report)
datasets.summary: Dollars the Department of Veterans Affairs paid in direct benefits in fiscal year 2025 in every U.S. county, from the Geographic Distribution of VA Expenditures (GDX) workbook of VA's National Center for Veterans Analysis and Statistics: disability compensation and veterans pension, dependency and indemnity compensation (DIC) and survivors pension, insurance, and specially adapted housing, with the total recomputed as the sum of the four (the workbook's Total column is a formula), and the compensation, pension and survivor dollars of the year before for the change. One record per county or county equivalent (3,223), per state, DC, Puerto Rico and Guam, for foreign countries, the Freely Associated States, other U.S. territories and unknown addresses, and for the US (187,660,338,257 dollars in all). Counties carry the Census FIPS code; Connecticut's counties are the planning regions.
datasets.uses: Use it to size a veterans' disability practice by money, not headcount: how many dollars of compensation and survivor benefits reach a county every year, how fast that is growing, and how a county compares with its state. Pair it with the va-compensation dataset (recipients by rating) by county FIPS code. Agents can look up a state and its counties, compare up to ten states, or search a county by name.

keywords: VA pension and survivor benefits by county
datasets.measurementTechnique: Read from VA's GDX workbook for the fiscal year (and the year before) cell for cell: the 'County Direct Exp', 'State Direct Exp' and 'CD Direct Exp' sheets. The workbook's Total column is a formula, so the total in each record is recomputed as the sum of the four direct categories and checked against the workbook's cached value. County rows are matched to vintage-2025 county FIPS codes in the shared crosswalks by state and county name (Connecticut's eight retired counties are listed with no dollars and are left out; its planning regions carry them). A gate re-reads fifty counties from the live workbook with a separate reader, checks that counties add up to VA's state rows and states to its Grand total, ties the Congressional District sheet (a separate cut of the same dollars) to each state, and holds dollars per recipient against the va-compensation dataset.

datasets.title: Vehicle safety complaints by state, make and model year (NHTSA complaint file)
datasets.summary: Safety complaints about cars, trucks, SUVs, motorcycles and RVs that owners filed with the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA), counted from its Office of Defects Investigation complaint file for the ten most recent model years, by the complainant's state, the make, the model year and the part of the vehicle named (engine, brakes, air bags, steering and the other NHTSA component groups). Each record gives the complaints, how many report a crash, a fire, an injury or a death, the people reported injured and killed, the complaints filed in the last twelve months, and how many concern a make, model and year that has a safety recall (and a recall of the same system), joined from NHTSA's recall file. State records list every make; make records add the model year by component table and each model's counts; national make records add each model by model year and the number of recall campaigns. A complaint is counted once however many parts it names. Only counts are kept: no narrative, VIN, city, name or complaint number.
datasets.uses: Use it to size the lemon-law and vehicle product-liability market in the states a firm serves: how many owners there complain about each make and model year, which systems they name, how many complaints involve a crash, a fire or an injury, and how many concern vehicles that were recalled. Look up a state to get every make, compare up to ten states, or search for a make such as Ford or a model such as Wrangler. Complaints are unverified owner reports, so read them as a signal of where owners have trouble, not as proof of a defect.

datasets.citation: Probative. (2026). Vehicle safety complaints by state, make and model year (NHTSA complaint file) (Version 2.0.0) [Data set]. Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23964283
datasets.citeAs: Probative Growth, Vehicle safety complaints by state, make and model year (NHTSA complaint file), 2026, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23964283
datasets.disclaimer: Not legal advice. These are counts of unverified complaints that vehicle owners filed with NHTSA, kept for research and marketing planning. A complaint is not a finding that a vehicle is defective, and a count says nothing about whether any owner has a lemon-law or injury claim. Rights and deadlines are for your own counsel.

datasets.measurementTechnique: NHTSA's ODI complaint flat file (FLAT_CMPL.zip, one row per component a complaint names) is read in full each month; vehicle complaints for the ten most recent model years are counted once per ODI number by the complainant's state, make, model, model year and component group, with crash, fire, injury and death flags, and joined to the ODI recall file (FLAT_RCL_POST_2010.zip) by make, model and model year. Totals are recounted from the file by a second parser and checked against NHTSA's public complaints API.

datasets.title: VA-accredited attorneys and claims agents per veteran, by state, with county counts and Board of Veterans' Appeals outcomes by type of representation
datasets.summary: How many attorneys and claims agents the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs has accredited to help with benefit claims, counted by the state (and, in the county file, the county) of each person's business address, against the VA's own projection of living veterans (VetPop2023, rounded to the nearest 1,000). One record per state, DC, Puerto Rico and territory, one for the United States and one for people whose list entry shows no US state, each with attorneys, claims agents, veterans per accredited attorney, accredited attorneys and agents per 100,000 veterans, the number accredited in the last 12 months and how many counties have none. Records for the Board of Veterans' Appeals add its decisions in fiscal year 2024 by outcome and by type of representative. The VA's lists name every person; only counts are read, and no name, phone number, registration number or ZIP code is published.
datasets.uses: Use it to see where VA-accredited attorneys and agents have offices compared with the veterans a state is projected to have, which counties have none, and how many were accredited recently, before you plan veterans' benefits marketing. Look up your state: the record gives the counts, the ratios and the history since this dataset began. The count is by business address, so it shows where offices are, not how many veterans each person serves, and the veteran counts are a projection.

datasets.mcpLine: VA-accredited attorneys and claims agents per veteran by state, county counts, and appeals outcomes by representation.
datasets.measurementTechnique: The VA Office of General Counsel's two complete lists (attorneys and claims agents) are downloaded with the same single form POST the page's Download button sends, parsed in memory and counted by the state in each business address, by county (the ZIP code's county in the Census ZCTA-to-county file) and by year accredited, then discarded; no name, phone, registration number or ZIP code is stored. Counts must add up to the lists' row counts, county counts to each state, and three states are matched against the VA's own search form. Veterans are VetPop2023 county rows (which add up to its state table) at the latest September 30, rounded to the nearest 1,000. The Board's table rows must add up to its grand total and its decision count.

datasets.title: Wage-and-hour and OSHA enforcement by county, state, act and industry (U.S. Department of Labor)
datasets.summary: What the U.S. Department of Labor found when it enforced wage and safety laws, counted by county, state and territory and for the US over the last ten complete federal fiscal years. From the Wage and Hour Division (WHD): concluded cases, cases with violations, back wages found owed, employees owed back wages, civil money penalties, Fair Labor Standards Act overtime and minimum wage back wages, and child labor violations. From the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA), federal and state-plan offices: inspections (and how many followed a complaint, a referral, an accident or a fatality or catastrophe), violations cited (serious, willful, repeat), and penalties. State and US records add one record per law WHD enforces (FLSA, FMLA, Davis-Bacon, the Service Contract Act, H-2A, H-2B, H-1B, MSPA and others) and one per industry sector. Only counts and sums are published: no employer name, address or case number, and back wages only where 3 or more employees were owed.
datasets.uses: Use it to size wage-and-hour and workplace-safety work in the counties a firm serves: how often federal investigators find unpaid wages there, how much is owed and to how many workers, which laws and industries the cases come from, and how many OSHA inspections follow a complaint, an accident or a death. Look up a state to get its county, law and industry records, compare up to ten states, or search for a county or an industry by name. These are the cases the federal government closed, not all wage theft or workplace injury: state labor agencies and private lawsuits are not in it.
datasets.attribution: Source: Probative, Wage-and-hour and OSHA enforcement by county, state, act and industry (U.S. Department of Labor), version 2.0.0, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23898146, licensed CC BY 4.0.

datasets.citeAs: Probative Growth, Wage-and-hour and OSHA enforcement by county, state, act and industry (U.S. Department of Labor), 2026, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23898146
datasets.disclaimer: Not legal advice. These are counts and sums of federal enforcement findings, kept for research and marketing planning. A WHD back-wage finding or an OSHA citation is the agency's finding, not a court judgment, and employers can contest them. Rights and deadlines in a wage or injury matter are for your own counsel.

keywords: Wage and Hour Division enforcement data
datasets.measurementTechnique: The DOL Open Data Portal's complete WHD enforcement, OSHA inspection and OSHA violation files are streamed and summed by state code, by county (the employer's or worksite's ZIP code placed with the Census ZCTA-to-county relationship file), by federal fiscal year (WHD by findings end date, OSHA by inspection open date), by law and by NAICS sector, without keeping any employer name, address or case number; deleted citation items and records of no inspection are left out. State totals computed straight from the state code are the totals gate, DOL's budget justifications (OSHA inspections) and WHD's fiscal-year tables (back wages) the second sources.

datasets.title: WARN Act layoff and closure notices by county: California and Texas
datasets.summary: How many mass-layoff and plant-closure notices employers filed under the Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification (WARN) Act, and how many employees they covered, for every county in the states whose workforce agencies publish the notices as files: California (July 2023 on, from the Employment Development Department's reports) and Texas (2019 on, from the Texas Workforce Commission's open-data table). Each county, state and county-not-given record carries the last 12 months, the last complete calendar year, the total since the file starts, and the month-by-month series. Only counts are kept: no employer name, address or contact. Notices are dated by the day the state agency received them. Other states are not included.
datasets.uses: Use it to see where layoffs are being announced: counties with a run of large notices have workers who may need an employment lawyer (final pay, severance, WARN notice-period claims, unemployment appeals), and a county with none is not necessarily quiet, because the file covers only two states and only employers large enough to be covered. Look up a state to get every county in it, compare the two states, or search by county name.

datasets.disclaimer: Not legal advice. These are counts of notices employers filed with state agencies, kept for research and marketing planning. A notice is a plan, not a layoff that has happened, and says nothing about whether any worker has a legal claim; rights and deadlines are for your own counsel.

datasets.title: Workers' compensation maximum weekly benefit by state: the cap on total-disability pay in each state
datasets.summary: The most a state pays each week in workers' compensation for total disability, for the injury period the state's own agency names. One row per state with the dollar figure, the period, the agency page or notice it comes from, and the verbatim sentence or table row.
datasets.uses: Use it to see how high a state's weekly workers' compensation benefit can go, for injury and workers' compensation work, and to quote the cap with its source. Maximums are reset on a schedule (January, July or October); each row names the period it covers and its date is when we last found the quote in the document.

datasets.title: Workplace injuries and fatal work injuries by state and industry (BLS SOII and CFOI)
datasets.summary: How often workers are hurt on the job in each state and industry, and how many die: the nonfatal injury and illness rate per 100 full-time workers for private-industry sectors and detailed industries in 42 states and DC (Survey of Occupational Injuries and Illnesses, 2024), and the number and rate of fatal work injuries in every state and DC, with the major cause and the industry rate (Census of Fatal Occupational Injuries, 2024). Every record carries its BLS series or table. Survey estimates carry a relative standard error and a noise flag, and every figure is the one BLS publishes. It is statistics about industries and states, never about a named employer.
datasets.uses: Use it to see which industries hurt workers most in a state, how a state's injury rate and fatal-injury rate compare with the nation, and what causes the deaths. Look up a state: each record gives the rate, the count, how precise the estimate is and the year-by-year trend. These are rates for whole industries, not for any one workplace, so they do not say whether a particular injury is covered by workers' compensation.
datasets.attribution: Source: Probative, Workplace injuries and fatal work injuries by state and industry (BLS SOII and CFOI), version 2.0.0, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23898154, licensed CC BY 4.0.
datasets.citation: Probative. (2026). Workplace injuries and fatal work injuries by state and industry (BLS SOII and CFOI) (Version 2.0.0) [Data set]. Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23898154
datasets.citeAs: Probative Growth, Workplace injuries and fatal work injuries by state and industry (BLS SOII and CFOI), 2026, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23898154
datasets.disclaimer: Not legal advice. These are survey and census statistics from the Bureau of Labor Statistics, kept for planning. A rate describes a whole industry in a state, not any one employer, and it does not say whether anyone has a workers' compensation claim.

datasets.mcpLine: Workplace injuries and fatal work injuries by state and industry, from BLS SOII and CFOI: rates, case counts and the riskiest sectors.
datasets.measurementTechnique: Nonfatal rates and case counts are read from the Bureau of Labor Statistics Survey of Occupational Injuries and Illnesses (SOII) time series IS by series id: total recordable cases, private industry, by state and industry, with the relative standard error. Fatal injury counts, causes and rates are read from the Census of Fatal Occupational Injuries (CFOI) state tables. Every record is a figure BLS publishes. Nothing is imputed and no employer is named.
